0x14044.why: the same carry and clamp as 0x13FCE, then splits the accumulator into whole = acc / divisor and a fraction acc mod divisor over the divisor, halves both until one is odd - lowest terms - special-cases 3/6 to 1/2, and returns whole in the high word, numerator in bits 8-15 and denominator in the low byte.

0x14138.name: take a count of ticks from the accumulator if there are that many
0x14138.why: adds the fractional byte at 0x3E3446 to the whole byte at 0x3E3448 and returns 0 if the total is below the requested count; otherwise decrements both until the count is met and returns 1. 0x1418A is the same question asked without taking anything, and 0x141C4 clears the fraction at 0x3E3446 and 0x3E3447.

0x14772.name: read one packed bookkeeping counter
0x14772.why: refuses an index above 0x16, so there are 23 counters, and takes the word at 0x1d616 + index*2 as a descriptor. The descriptor packs three things: (d5 >> 5) & 0x7f is the counter's offset in NIBBLES into the packed array at 0x3e34cc, ((d5 >> 12) & 3) + 1 is its length in nibbles, and the low five bits are a display slot the writer uses. It then assembles the value nibble by nibble from 0x3e34cc, with a separate path for an odd starting nibble. Nothing here touches a sound chip; the derived name `lookUpSoundRequestUnpack` is wrong.

0x14dd2.name: step all eight sound envelopes
0x14dd2.why: eight passes of soundEnvelopeStep's helper at 0x14B2C with the index in the frame long at -4.

0x14e5c.name: clear and rebuild all twelve sound channel blocks
0x14e5c.why: six times round: fillBytesLongCount zeroes 0x14 bytes at the cursor, then two calls to soundChannelDispatch with 0x3E3536 and the next two channel numbers, the cursor stepping 0xA each time from 0x3E3454. Twelve channels of ten bytes.

0x14f7a.name: clear one of the six twenty-byte channel blocks
0x14f7a.why: rejects an index of 6 or more with -1, then addresses `0x3E3454 + index * 0x14` and clears its twenty bytes.

0x1540a.name: draw the title's version line
0x1540a.why: writes 0x78 into the word at 0x3E361E, floors it at 3, calls 0x18B26 with 0x1A, 0xF, that word, 3, 1 and 0x20, then plots the string at 0x1D6B4. Every argument is an immediate, so the two addresses are the whole of what it does.

0x15504.name: format a number and draw it left-trimmed
0x15504.why: `link a6,#-12` for the buffer, formatNumberPaddingSeparators into it with width 0xB, then walks past the leading 0x20 spaces and hands the first non-space to stringLengthWrapper with the caller's two sign-extended bytes as its position.

0x1586a.name: run the self-test entry the index names, if there is one
0x1586a.why: indexes the long table at 0x1DAF8 by the caller's word; a zero entry means nothing to do, otherwise it runs four steps from there.

0x1594c.name: the service menu screen, one entry per page
0x1594c.why: at 1,200 bytes the third largest routine here, and it is a screen painter: stringLengthWrapper at 0x17FCC, selfTestResultAccumulate at 0x1851C and bitfieldExtract at 0x18B76 are held in registers, and the frame words at -4 and -8 are the page and the row.

0x15dfc.name: scale the sound request's three fields and divide
0x15dfc.why: returns zero when soundEnableCheck says the driver is off; otherwise looks up requests 0xB, 0xA and 0x9, adds the last two to the first, and computes `x*4` then `(x*4)*16 - x*4` - sixty times the sum - before handing it and the enable result to dualDivideHelper.

0x15e50.name: scale a sound request by two others and the enable answer
0x15e50.why: soundEnableCheck for the enable, then requests 0xC and 3, and the caller's two words as the scale. The sibling of 0x15DFC, which uses requests 0xB, 0xA and 9.

0x15f3e.name: show the coin and credit page of the service menu
0x15f3e.why: selfTestResultAccumulate at 0x1851C and stringLengthWrapper at 0x17FCC held in registers, and it branches on bit 24 of the accumulator's answer before drawing.

0x16148.name: draw one service-menu row from a packed byte
0x16148.why: the row byte's high nibble is the column and its low nibble the field width, and the caller's two words are the position. Three fields to a row - `moveq #$2,d5`.

0x16358.name: the operator adjustments page, one row per setting
0x16358.why: at 1,268 bytes the second largest routine in the upper image. stringLengthWrapper and skipNthRecordPackedList at 0x160F8 are its two tools, 0x1622A the string table, and the byte at 0x372 selects between two layouts.

0x16af8.name: draw the service screen's frame and title
0x16af8.why: recordWhetherVectorHoldsStub, the two nested borders at 0x174A2, and soundTableInit, then the title string at 0x1E252 at position 0x2030 when the caller's word is set.

0x16d78.name: run the self test, then back to the service menu
0x16d78.why: `bsr.w $17800` - selfTestMain - then `bra.w $16fe0`, the tail every case of this jump table returns through.

0x16d80.name: run the routine at 0x16FF0, then back to the service menu
0x16d80.why: `bsr.w $16ff0; bra.w $16fe0`. One call and the shared tail; the callee is still an address, so this name can only say which.

0x16e14.name: run the routine at 0x175DE, then back to the service menu

0x16e1c.name: show the self-test detail screen, then back to the service menu

0x16e24.name: accumulate the self-test result, then back to the service menu

0x16e2c.name: run the seven-step input test
0x16e2c.why: blitParameterSetup with 7, then walks the seven word entries of 0x1E454 as the labels for each step.

0x16eec.name: run the sixteen-step switch test
0x16eec.why: the sibling of 0x16E2C with a count of 0x10 and the label table at 0x1E45E.

0x16ff0.name: the service menu's main loop
0x16ff0.why: draws the frame through 0x16AF8, then loops on selfTestResultBranch at 0x1796E with bitfieldExtract, selfTestResultAccumulate and waitUntilLongChanges held in registers. This is what the menu's jump table cases return to.

0x17330.name: draw the two-column diagnostic readout
0x17330.why: two calls to bitfieldExtract, the first with 0xF, 9 and the string at 0x1DDB6 at colour 0x2000, the second with 4 and a zero string.

0x173d8.name: draw the burn-in screen's frame and its two lines
0x173d8.why: the same frame as 0x16AF8 - 0x17500, the borders, soundTableInit - then the strings at 0x1E16A at 0x2030 and 0x1E012 at 0x2040.

0x174a2.name: draw the two nested frame borders in colour 0x0101
0x174a2.why: eight passes of 0xA8 columns writing 0x101 at the top of the screen and 0x1CC00 below it - the outer border - then 0xE6 passes of four writing at +2 and +0x148 with a 0x1F8 stride, which is the inner one. Both coordinates and the colour are immediates.

0x175de.name: the colour bars page of the service menu
0x175de.why: draws the frame and banner, then writes a colour straight into the palette at 0x3C003C through 0x1829C with 0x39EF, with bitfieldExtract and the chain plotter held in registers.

0x17b04.name: read the two switch words and decide which page to show
0x17b04.why: waitUntilLongChanges, then two calls to selfTestResultAccumulate - the second with 0x30000F0 - and masks the answer with 0x3000000 to see whether both service switches are held.

0x17bf6.name: nudge the record's two words by the four direction bits
0x17bf6.why: bits 7 and 6 of d5 add and subtract 0x80 on the word at +6; bits 5 and 4 do the same to the word at +4. Four independent tests, one per direction, and 0x80 is the step.

0x17c2c.name: index the string table at 0x1DEF0 by the record's packed field
0x17c2c.why: the word at +6 gives a row in bits 4 to 6 - `and 0x70` then `asr` - and a column in bits 0 to 2, and their sum indexes the table.

0x17cb8.name: step the record's low three bits by the flag, wrapping within them
0x17cb8.why: bit 7 of d4 adds one to the low three bits of the word at +6, keeping the rest with `andi.w #$fff8`, so the field wraps at eight. The three-bit sibling of the four-bit 0x17D2C.

0x17d2c.name: step the record's low nibble up or down by the flag bits
0x17d2c.why: bit 7 of d4 adds one to the low nibble of the word at +4, bit 6 subtracts one, and neither leaves it alone; the top twelve bits are put back unchanged with `andi.w #$fff0`, so the nibble wraps within itself.

0x17d58.name: flip the sign bit of the record's word when the two owner bits are set
0x17d58.why: `andi.l #$c0,d0` on the value moved through a0 - the owner bits - and `eori.w #$8000,$2(a2)` only when they are non-zero.

0x17d6e.name: step the record index by the flag bits, within its list
0x17d6e.why: bit 7 of d4 counts d3 down when it is not already zero; bit 6 counts it up, but only when the word a2 points at is exactly one past it - the end of the list. Either way the new index is scaled by eight and added to the base in a3.

0x17d9c.name: draw the adjustment row's label, value and units
0x17d9c.why: three calls through a4 with colour 0x2000 at columns 0x16, 0x14 and 3, the middle one carrying the sign-extended value in d3. The tail every case of the adjustment page branches to.

0x17f42.name: blit the two text tables at 0x1DFB2 and 0x1E034
0x17f42.why: two identical calls to stringLengthWrapper at 0x17FCC, each with 0xFFFF, a row number - 0x1B then 0x1C - a table address and 0x2040. Consecutive rows of the same screen.

0x18040.name: write a long as two palette entries
0x18040.why: splits the caller's long with `lsr.l #$10` and passes each half to 0x1829C, which writes one colour into the first palette.

0x181a4.name: call 0x18040 with 0x30 and the constant 0x3DE07BC0
0x181a4.why: `pea $3de07bc0.l; pea $30.w; bsr.w $18040; addq.l #$8,a7`. Two pushed constants and one call; the meaning is the callee's.

0x181b6.name: clear the whole palette to entry zero
0x181b6.why: walks two counters from zero calling 0x1829C for each, so every entry is written with the same colour.

0x1830c.name: draw the eight-byte switch state at 0x3E367C
0x1830c.why: indexes the byte block at 0x3E367C by the caller's long and draws it at colour 0x2020, position 2 - one row of the switch display.

0x18658.name: halt on an unhandled vector
0x18658.why: `jmp $1e8d2.l`, which is the `stop #$2700` in the upper image. Reached through the exception vector table, so an entry that lands here stops the machine with every interrupt masked.

0x18764.name: step the glyph layer's frame counters
0x18764.why: the layer state lives at 0x3e3400: word 4 counts up every call and word 2 is tested for zero, which is what decides whether the per-slot work below runs at all.

0x1884a.name: release the slot and take its record
0x1884a.why: `clr.b $18(a2,d2.w)` marks the slot free, `movea.l $34(a2,d0.w),a0` takes the record pointer and `clr.l` drops it, then into the shared tail at 0x1886A. The teardown case of the 0x3E3400 table's jump table.

0x1885a.name: toggle the slot's blink flag and draw or erase it
0x1885a.why: `tst.b $2c(a2,d2.w)` picks the branch: set, it is cleared and the record goes to 0x18D18; clear, it is set to 1 and the record goes to 0x18A66 with the slot's word at +0x10. Both rejoin the frame walk at 0x18902, so this is one slot alternating between two treatments every time round.

0x1888c.name: step the slot's repeat count and run its script
0x1888c.why: reads the byte at +0x30 of the slot, increments it in place, picks the word at +0x10 and the record pointer at +0x34, and calls scriptInterpreterStep at 0x18C48 with the old count in d0.

0x188aa.name: run the slot's script test, and advance to the next record when it fails
0x188aa.why: steps the slot's repeat count at +0x30 and calls scriptInterpreterTest at 0x18CAA; a non-zero answer returns to the frame walk. A zero one takes the record's byte at +6 plus the word at 0x3E3400, and either frees the slot when that has run out or follows the chain pointer at +8 and resets the repeat count.

0x188ec.name: run the handler for the slot's record and rejoin the frame step
0x188ec.why: `add.w d0,d0; movea.l $34(a2,d0.w),a0` picks the slot's record pointer out of the 0x3E3400 block, `bsr.w $18940` runs it, and `bra.b $18902` returns to the per-frame walk in 0x18764.

0x188f8.name: run the slot's record handler, then finish the frame walk
0x188f8.why: `add.w d0,d0; movea.l $34(a2,d0.w),a0; bsr.w $189a0` then the `dbra` that ends 0x18764's four-slot loop and its epilogue. The sibling of 0x188EC, which calls 0x18940 instead and rejoins mid-loop.

0x18940.name: rotate one row or column of the glyph grid by a cell
0x18940.why: 0x3E340E picks which: set, it walks a column upward with a 0xC0 stride over 0x1D cells, carrying the first word round to the end; clear, it shifts a row of 0x1F words left and wraps the first into the last. The row or column is the record's byte at +1, and the chain is followed by the byte at +6 plus 0x3E3400 and the pointer at +8.

0x189a0.name: scroll the glyph grid a row up, or copy it back down
0x189a0.why: one entry moves 0x29 words at a time backwards with `move.w -(a0),-(a1)` over 0x1E rows, striding 0x92, clearing the vacated word; the other copies 0x20 words forwards over 0x1D rows and clears a final row of 0x20. The two halves of scrolling a 0x92-byte-pitch grid.

0x18a06.name: scroll the whole glyph grid one cell, in whichever direction 0x3E340E says
0x18a06.why: set, it walks backwards over 0x1E rows of 0x29 words with a 0x92 stride, clearing the word each row vacates; clear, it copies 0x1D rows of 0x20 words forwards and clears a final row. The whole-grid version of the single row or column at 0x18940.

0x18a5e.name: take a pointer and a width, then plot a glyph string
0x18a5e.why: `move.w $a(a7),d1; movea.l $4(a7),a0` and falls into the body at 0x18A66, which is what 0x18E06 also calls. Two arguments off the stack and nothing else; the work is all in the body.

0x18a66.name: plot a glyph string, clipping to the visible rows
0x18a66.why: reads two bytes as the position, adds the scroll offset at 0x3E3406 to the row, and skips the string entirely when that falls outside 0..0x2A. 0x40 in a1 is the row pitch. This is the body 0x18A5E and 0x18E06 both enter.

0x18c3c.name: take a pointer, a width and a count, then plot a glyph string
0x18c3c.why: `move.w $a(a7),d1; movea.l $4(a7),a0; move.w $e(a7),d0` and falls through. One argument more than 0x18A5E, which sets up the same body.

0x18cce.name: take a cell and a colour, then address the playfield
0x18cce.why: `move.w $e(a7),d0; move.w $12(a7),d1; andi.w #$30f0,d1` and falls into 0x18CDE, the eight-by-eight cell address routine. The 0x30F0 mask is the same colour mask the glyph plotters use.

0x18d18.name: decompress the chain's tiles into the playfield
0x18d18.why: computes a playfield address from the record's two bytes - `(b0 << 3) + (b1 >> 4)` biased by 0x200004 - then feeds each byte of the string at +2 to decompressTileId with 0x33 and 0x1000, threading the returned address into the next call. Follows the chain by the byte at +6 plus 0x3E3400 and the pointer at +8, exactly as the plotters do.

0x18dea.name: claim a slot at 0x3E3400 with kind four, clearing the caller's word
0x18dea.why: `moveq #$4,d0; move.w $a(a7),d1; clr.w $a(a7)` and into 0x18E06's body. The only entry that zeroes the caller's argument on the way in, and one of the two kinds 0x18E06 does not run 0x18A66 for.

0x18df6.name: claim a slot at 0x3E3400 with kind two

0x18dfc.name: claim a slot with kind one
0x18dfc.why: two instructions - `moveq #1,d0` and the branch into the shared claim - so the kind is the only thing this entry decides.

0x18e06.name: claim one of the four slots at 0x3E3400 and fill it
0x18e06.why: scans the four bytes at 0x3E3415..0x3E3418 downward with `tst.b -(a1)` / `dbeq` for a zero, returns 0 if all four are busy. Fills the slot's parallel fields - the byte at +0x2c set to 1 and +0x30 cleared, the words at +0x1c, +0x24 and +0x10, the long at +0x34 - runs 0x18A66 for kinds 1 and 2 only, writes the kind byte into the slot and returns 1.

0x18e66.name: plot a chain of strings and return the width drawn
0x18e66.why: reads two bytes as a cell address into the playfield at 0x200004, and when bit 1 of the flags is set walks the string to the first comma or space to right-align it, filling sixteen rows of a column with (flags & 0xF0) + 5 as the colour. Then plots each byte through the translation table at 0x192E6 and 0x18F10, adding up the widths, and follows the chain by the count at 0x3E3400 and the pointer at +2.

0x18f10: format a number into the glyph buffer

0x19010.name: draw a glyph run down a column
0x19010.why: the same as 0x19032 but with a0 = 0xFFFE0080: a step of 0x80 bytes, which is one row of the 64-word-wide glyph grid, and a paired write two bytes back.

0x19032.name: draw a glyph run into the 0x800002 window
0x19032.why: 0x19010 instruction for instruction, with one difference: a0 is 0x800002 here and 0xfffe0080 there. Both mask the attribute word to 0x30f0, index the same PC-relative byte table at 0x192e6 by the glyph number, and branch to the same 0x18f10 - so the destination window is the entire choice between them.

0x19054.name: format a value through the scaled converter and draw it
0x19054.why: formats into a 16-byte buffer on its own frame and falls THROUGH into the shared tail at 0x190a2, which 0x1908a also enters - so the two are one routine with two heads. This head uses the converter at 0x1946e and pushes 0x64 as its third argument, which is the ASCII letter 'd' - 0x1946e is a printf conversion and that byte selects decimal, NOT a scale of a hundred, which is what an earlier version of this note said. 0x1908a's head uses the plain formatter at 0x19614 instead. Before converting it sets bit 1 of the byte at 0x1e(a6) always and bit 2 of it when bit 1 of the argument at 0x18(a6) is clear, so it modifies a flags byte IN the caller's frame - which is why that argument is absent from the params table. The tail draws through 0x18e66 where 0x18b26 draws through 0x18a5e.

0x1908a.name: format a number with separators into a local buffer and plot it
0x1908a.why: the same sixteen-byte local buffer as 0x19054, filled by 0x19614 - the decimal formatter that groups digits - and plotted with 0x18E66.

0x190c0.name: format a number in a power-of-two base into a local buffer and plot it
0x190c0.why: `link a6,#-16`, 0x195B4 to fill the buffer with digits, then the shared plot tail at 0x190A2. The sibling of 0x19054 and 0x1908A, differing only in which formatter fills the buffer.

0x190da.name: plot a chain of strings with the caller's colour byte
0x190da.why: moves the byte at $7(a7) into the colour slot at $a(a7), clears $10(a7), and calls 0x18E66 with the flags word. Argument shuffling and one call.

0x190f6.name: erase a chain of glyph runs and return how many cells were cleared
0x190f6.why: the same walk as 0x18E66 - orientation from 0x3E340E, cell address from two bytes, chain followed by the count at 0x3E3400 - but each character becomes `clr.w (a1)` and `clr.w (a1,d2.w)` rather than a glyph. It clears one extra cell for characters outside 0x27..0x2E, and returns the count.

0x1939c.name: clear the glyph layer's state block at 0x3E3400
0x1939c.why: clears the words at 0x3E3400, 0x3E3402, 0x3E3406, 0x3E3408 and 0x3E340A, then the four slot bytes from 0x3E3418 and the four longs from 0x3E3434 - exactly the fields 0x18E06 fills.

0x193f2.name: store two bytes at a pointer and clear the byte four past them
0x193f2.why: `move.b $b(a7),(a0)+; move.b $f(a7),(a0)+; clr.b $4(a0)`. Three fields of a record the caller points at, and nothing else.

0x19404.name: clear a kilobyte of the playfield from a row offset
0x19404.why: `move.w #$3ff,d0` then the shared loop at 0x1940E, which fills longs from 0x200004 plus (the byte argument << 12). 0x1940A is the same loop entered with 0x7FF, which is why that one is named for eight kilobytes.

0x1946e.name: convert one value according to a printf conversion letter
0x1946e.why: the byte at 0xf(a7) is an ASCII CONVERSION LETTER and the routine is a printf %-spec in one piece: 0x64 'd' and 0x73 's' each branch to their own path, and the rest fall into a common integer path whose base is set by the letter - 0x58 'X', 0x78 'x' and 0x68 'h' give four bits a digit with a mask of 0xf, 0x6f 'o' gives three and 7, and anything else gives one and 1, which is binary. The 0x27 against 7 in d5 is the difference between 'A'-'F' and 'a'-'f'. The 's' path emits 0x2b '+' or, for a negative value, negates it and emits 0x2d '-' before falling on.

0x19552.name: choose the sign character and the group mask for the field
0x19552.why: picks a group mask out of the table at 0x1959C by the field index, and for a conversion that is not 'd' (0x64) takes the character already at the buffer head and writes a space over it - the sign the caller placed. Both go into d1, one half each, for the emit loop.

0x19572.name: emit one copy of the byte, or two when the mask bit is set
0x19572.why: `add.w d1,d1` shifts the next group-width bit out of the mask; on a carry an extra `move.b d0,(a0)+` runs before the ordinary one. The separator step of the grouped number formatter.

0x1957a.name: copy the digits out, inserting a separator where the mask says
0x1957a.why: walks the formatted digits, skipping leading 0x20 spaces, emitting the sign byte held in the high half of d1 once, and shifting the group mask in the low half - a carry emits 0x2C before the next digit, a zero ends the run. The table it reads the mask from is at 0x1959E, which is what capstone shows as instructions after the `rts`.

0x195b4.name: convert a long to digits in a power-of-two base, right aligned
0x195b4.why: d3 digits' worth of bits at a time, masked with d4, +0x30 for '0'..'9' and +d5 more when the digit is 10 or above - 7 gives 'A'..'F' and 0x27 gives 'a'..'f'. Written backwards from the end of a field of the given width with `move.b d2,-(a0)`, so the result is right aligned.

0x1960a.name: pad the field with spaces and return
0x1960a.why: `moveq #$20,d1` then `move.b d1,-(a0)` under a `dbra`, filling backwards to the start of the field with 0x20, and into the exit at 0x19604. The left padding of the number formatter.

0x19614.name: format a number with padding and separators
0x19614.why: digits are produced back to front from the end of the buffer - divu #$a, swap, add 0x30, move.b d1,-(a0) - which is decimal, and the buffer is the pointer at 0xc(a7) with the width at 0x12(a7), null-terminated at that width before anything is written. Values above 0x1869f, which is 99,999, are halved and divided by 0xc350 first so the top half survives a 16-bit divu, with addx putting the halving back. Bit 31 of d2 is set when the word at 0x16(a7) is zero and is what makes the loop keep going past a zero quotient - so that argument is the pad-with-zeroes flag. Every sixth position is skipped by the subq.w #$6 path, which is where a separator goes. When it is 1 the leading spaces are stripped by copying the string down, and otherwise the head is filled with 0x20.

0x19786.name: start the divide helper with a zero high word
0x19786.why: `suba.l a0,a0` for a zero a0, saves d3, moves the argument into it, and joins the body at 0x197A0.

0x197f4.name: round the quotient by half the divisor, keeping the sign
0x197f4.why: halves the caller's word with `asr.w #$1`, makes it positive, flips its sign to match the dividend's, and adds it before the division - which is how this ROM rounds to nearest rather than truncating.

0x1994c.name: branch to the d2/d3/a2/a3 epilogue
0x1994c.why: `bra.w $19a1e` and nothing else: an exit path that exists at its own address so a jump table can name it.

0x19950.name: branch into the routine at 0x19966
0x19950.why: `bra.w $19966` and nothing else - an entry point that exists so a caller has an address for a place inside another routine.

0x19954.name: write a byte to the sound chip with interrupts held off
0x19954.why: saves sr, raises the mask to 7 with `ori.w #$700,sr`, pokes the saved status byte at 0x5AFFFF and the value at (a1,d0.w), then restores sr. The critical section is the point: the write pair must not be interrupted.

0x19966.name: branch into the routine at 0x1997C
0x19966.why: `bra.w $1997c`; what follows in the extent does not decode as a continuation of it. An entry point at its own address, like 0x19950.

0x19a1e.name: restore d2, d3, a2 and a3, then return
0x19a1e.why: `movem.l (a7)+,d2-d3/a2-a3; rts` - a shared epilogue several routines in the sound driver branch to.

0x19a24.name: expand one row of a compressed sprite, inverted
0x19a24.why: the record's byte at +5 is the row width; the source advances by it and the destination by twice the product with the row number, and each byte is complemented with `not.b` as it goes.

0x19b06.name: expand a compressed sprite two pixels at a time
0x19b06.why: returns at once on a null pointer at (a2), biases the destination by the word at +4, and walks the width at +5 of the record halving it with `lsr.b #$1` - two pixels to a byte.

0x19bb8.name: take a destination and a source pointer off the stack
0x19bb8.why: `movea.l $4(a7),a1; move.l a1,d0; movea.l $8(a7),a0` and falls through. Two arguments and a copy of one into d0; the work is in what follows.

0x19c2e.name: trap and halt
0x19c2e.why: `trap #$0` then `stop #$2700`. The fatal path - called from exceptionReporter and from the sound driver's own error branches - and it does not return.

0x19c34.name: reset the bus and restart through the reset vector
0x19c34.why: `reset` asserts the chip's reset line to the rest of the board, then `suba.l a0,a0; movea.l (a0)+,a7; jmp (a0)` restarts from the first eight bytes of the image. Harder than 0x1E9B4, which restarts the processor alone.

0x19c70.name: track two axes and record the direction each has just reversed in
0x19c70.why: for each of two bytes: copies the current value down, subtracts the previous, and compares the sign of the difference with the byte holding the last one - writing the new difference into the field two further on only when the sign has changed or gone to zero. Fields 0, 2, 4, 6 for the first axis and 1, 3, 5, 7 for the second.

0x19ccc.name: swap the halves of d1
0x19ccc.why: `moveq #$30,d0; rol.l d0,d1` - a rotate of 48, which on a longword is a rotate of 16, so the two halves change places. Falls through into what follows.

0x19f3e.name: initialise the sixteen records at 0x3E370E and their rings
0x19f3e.why: links sixteen 0x60-byte records head to tail by storing each one's successor at its own offset zero, clearing the fields at +8, +0x14, +0x16, +0x24, +0x25 and +0x5F of each; terminates the last with a zero long; clears thirteen longs at 0x3E3D12; and points the two ring pairs at 0x3E3D56/0x3E3D5A and 0x3E3D62/0x3E3D66 at 0x3E3D46 and 0x3E3D5E.

0x1a05a.name: clear a ring's head, or link a record into it
0x1a05a.why: the first entry clears the bytes at +8 and +0xA and the long at +4 - an empty ring. The second writes the caller's pointer into +4 and, when it is not null, threads the record it names on after it.

0x1a1ca.name: dispatch a channel command through the twenty-two-way table at 0x1A204
0x1a1ca.why: indexes the ten-byte records at 0x1B674 by the command byte - `d0*2` then `d0*4 + that`, which is ten - takes the opcode byte from the record, rejects anything above 0x15 to the command tail at 0x1A3E0, and jumps through the word table. a2 is pointed at the sixteen records at 0x3E370E first, so every case has them to hand.

0x1a230.name: store the command's byte into 0x3E36E8
0x1a230.why: `move.b $1(a1),$3e36e8` and back to the command tail at 0x1A3E0. One byte of the command into one global.

0x1a23c.name: store the command's byte through its own pointer
0x1a23c.why: `movea.l $6(a1),a0; move.b $1(a1),(a0)` and back to 0x1A3E0. The command carries both the value at +1 and where to put it at +6.

0x1a248.name: add the command's byte through its own pointer
0x1a248.why: `movea.l $6(a1),a0; move.b $1(a1),d0; add.b d0,(a0)` and back to 0x1A3E0. The additive sibling of 0x1A23C.

0x1a256.name: call through the pointer at offset 6 of the command
0x1a256.why: `movea.l $6(a1),a0; jsr (a0)` then `bra.w $1a3e0`, the tail every case of this command table returns through. The command carries its own handler.

0x1a260.name: mark every record whose field 0x15 matches the command's byte
0x1a260.why: walks the sixteen 0x60-byte records, comparing `$15(a2,d0.w)` against the byte at +1 of the command and writing 0xFF into `$12(a2,d0.w)` on a match, then back to the command tail at 0x1A3E0.

0x1a284.name: mark every record whose field 0x12 matches, when the command is kind eight
0x1a284.why: indexes the ten-byte command records by the byte at +1, requires the opcode there to be 8, and then walks the sixteen 0x60-byte records writing 0xFF into `$12(a2,d0.w)` wherever it already equals the command's byte at +2.

0x1a2c6.name: mark every record on the list the command's two nibbles select
0x1a2c6.why: splits the byte at +1 into two nibbles: the high one indexes the six-byte records at 0x19CE4 and its field +5 is added to the low one, and that sum indexes the thirteen list heads at 0x3E3D12. It then walks the list, writing 0xFF into each record's field 0x12 and following the link at offset zero.

0x1a318.name: silence every channel running this script
0x1a318.why: the command's byte at 1 times ten indexes the record table in a3, and the entry must be kind 8. Its byte at 2 is then compared against byte 0x12 of each of the sixteen channels, and silencing a channel here is always the same four writes: byte 0x5c cleared, word 0x58 set to 0x100, word 0x5a to 0xd000 and byte 0x12 to 0xfe, the finishing marker - at 0x60 bytes a channel across sixteen of them.

0x1a58a.name: read the channel's value, from the table above six or the jump table below
0x1a58a.why: a selector of 6 or more indexes the bytes at 0x3E36AC by selector minus six and sign-extends; below six it jumps through the five-way table at 0x1A5BE, whose cases are the field reads at 0x1A5C8 to 0x1A5E0. Anything above four in that range falls to the field 0x5E read at 0x1A5E6.

0x1a5c8.name: read the word at offset 0x1C and shift it right three
0x1a5c8.why: `move.w $1c(a0),d0; lsr.w #$3,d0; andi.b #$ff,d0` and into signExtendByteLong at 0x1A5EA - so the top five bits of the field become the answer.

0x1a5d4.name: sign-extend the byte at offset 0x19 of the record
0x1a5d4.why: `move.b $19(a0),d0; bra.b $1a5ea` - one field read and the shared sign extension. A jump-table case; the offset is what the case selects.

0x1a5da.name: sign-extend the byte at offset 0x1B of the record

0x1a5e0.name: sign-extend the byte at offset 0x16 of the record

0x1a5e6.name: sign-extend the byte at offset 0x5E of the record
0x1a5e6.why: `move.b $5e(a0),d0` and falls into signExtendByteLong at 0x1A5EA. The offset is the whole routine.

0x1a5ea.name: sign extend byte to long
0x1a5ea.why: ext.w d0, ext.l d0, rts. Three instructions and no memory: the byte in d0 widened to a long with its sign, which is what a caller that has just done a move.b into d0 needs before using it as an index or an offset.

0x1a5f0.name: run one channel's script to its next rest
0x1a5f0.why: clears the flag at 0x3E36EC and keeps the record in the frame, then enters the script reader's loop at 0x1B054 with 0x3E36E2 and 0x3E36DA - the note table and the current instrument - in registers.

0x1a704.name: raise flag bit one and clear the two counters at 0x3E3706
0x1a704.why: `ori.b #$2,(a4)` then `clr.w` into 0x3E3706 and a zero byte into 0x3E3708, and out through 0x1B050.

0x1a71a.name: quarter the record's word at 0x22, or clear the counters
0x1a71a.why: with the word at +8 zero it falls to 0x1B050 or to 0x1A704 depending on the frame long; otherwise, when neither of bits 1 and 2 of 0x3E36D4 is set, `asr.w #$2` halves the word at +0x22 twice.

0x1a740.name: total the channel's pitch, offset and bend into the long at d5
0x1a740.why: the word at +8 always; and when the frame long is set, the words at +0x1C and +0x22 as well. The three components of a channel's final pitch.

0x1a808.name: clear the frame byte five below a6, then continue at 0x1B048
0x1a808.why: `clr.b -$5(a6); bra.w $1b048`. One field of the caller's frame and a tail jump.

0x1a810.name: read two script bytes and dispatch opcodes 0x80 to 0xBB
0x1a810.why: takes two bytes through the cursor at +4 of the record, stepping it each time, and jumps through the word table at 0x1A848 for a first byte between 0x80 and 0xBB; anything else goes to 0x1AE44. The second byte is left in d4, which is the operand every case there reads.

0x1abc6.name: copy field 0x5d into field 0x5e
0x1abc6.why: one move and the jump back; the four entries above it all arrive here.

0x1abf6.name: take the next byte of the script and step its pointer
0x1abf6.why: `movea.l $4(a2),a0; addq.l #$1,$4(a2); moveq #$0,d3; move.b (a0),d3` - reads through the cursor at +4 of the record and advances it, which is what makes this a script reader rather than a field read.

0x1ac02.name: read a three-byte big-endian operand from the script
0x1ac02.why: three passes of `movea.l $4(a2),a0; addq.l #$1,$4(a2); move.b (a0),d0` shifted by 8, 0x10 and 0 into d3 - the cursor at +4 stepping once per byte, most significant first.

0x1ace0.name: sign-extend field 0x5D of the record into the word at 0x1C

0x1acec.name: copy field 0x5D of the record into field 0x19
0x1acec.why: `move.b $5d(a2),$19(a2); bra.w $1b048`. One field to another and the shared tail.

0x1acf6.name: sign-extend field 0x5D of the record into the word at 0x1A
0x1acf6.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d1; ext.w d1; move.w d1,$1a(a2)`. Field 0x1A where 0x1ACE0 writes 0x1C.

0x1ad04.name: copy field 0x5D into 0x16 unless field 0x12 is 0xFE
0x1ad04.why: `cmpi.b #$fe,$12(a2)` returns straight to the tail; otherwise `move.b $5d(a2),$16(a2)` and then the same `tst.l -$a(a6)` branch to 0x1A90E that 0x1AD6E makes.

0x1ad20.name: dispatch on d4 through the five-way table at 0x1AD38
0x1ad20.why: `cmpi.w #$4,d1` rejects anything above four straight to the tail, then `jmp $1ad38(pc,d1.w)` through a word table of relative offsets. The script opcode's sub-dispatch.

0x1ad42.name: subtract sign-extended field 0x5D from the word at 0x1C, and mark
0x1ad42.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d1; ext.w d1; sub.w d1,$1c(a2)` then `ori.b #$1,(a4)`, which is the tail 0x1ACE0 also branches to - so every write to that word raises the same flag bit.

0x1ad54.name: add field 0x5D of the record to field 0x19
0x1ad54.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d4; add.b d4,$19(a2); bra.w $1b048`. The additive sibling of 0x1ACEC, which copies rather than adds.

0x1ad60.name: add sign-extended field 0x5D to the word at 0x1A
0x1ad60.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d1; ext.w d1; add.w d1,$1a(a2)`. The additive sibling of 0x1ACF6.

0x1ad6e.name: add field 0x5D to field 0x16, and run 0x1A90E if the frame long is set
0x1ad6e.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d4; add.b d4,$16(a2)` then a `tst.l -$a(a6)`: zero takes the ordinary tail at 0x1B048, non-zero jumps to 0x1A90E instead.

0x1ad82.name: run the script's test and store the result in fields 0x5D and 0x5E
0x1ad82.why: the same call to 0x1A58A the branching cases make, but the byte it returns is written to both fields rather than tested.

0x1ad9a.name: read field 0x5D of the record and shift it right by d4
0x1ad9a.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d0; asr.b d4,d0; bra.b $1ada8` - a jump-table case whose whole content is which field it reads and that it shifts arithmetically.

0x1ada2.name: shift field 0x5D of the record left by d4
0x1ada2.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d0; asl.b d4,d0; move.b d0,$5d(a2)` - and the store is the tail 0x1AD9A branches to, so the right shift there writes the field back through this instruction.

0x1adb0.name: run the script's test and skip a longword when it is zero
0x1adb0.why: the same call as 0x1ADCC; a non-zero result carries on reading the script, a zero one does `addq.l #$4,$4(a2)` first - stepping the cursor past the four bytes of the branch it did not take.

0x1adcc.name: run the script's test and branch on any non-zero result
0x1adcc.why: pushes the record and d4, calls 0x1A58A, and takes the loop back to 0x1ABF6 - the script reader - only when the result is zero; otherwise 0x1ADC4. The three cases 0x1ADCC, 0x1ADE2 and 0x1ADF8 differ in nothing but the condition they branch on.

0x1ade2.name: run the script's test and branch when the result is negative
0x1ade2.why: identical to 0x1ADCC but for `bge.w` where that has `bne.b`, so this continues reading the script when the result is zero or positive.

0x1adf8.name: run the script's test and branch when the result is not negative
0x1adf8.why: identical to 0x1ADCC but for `blt.w`, the opposite of 0x1ADE2.

0x1ae0e.name: set field 0x5E to field 0x5D less the script's test result
0x1ae0e.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d3`, calls 0x1A58A, `sub.b d0,d3; move.b d3,$5e(a2)`. The computed sibling of 0x1AE2A, which subtracts d4 instead.

0x1ae2a.name: set field 0x5E to field 0x5D less d4
0x1ae2a.why: `move.b $5d(a2),d0; moveq #$0,d2; move.b d4,d2; sub.b d2,d0; move.b d0,$5e(a2)`.

0x1ae3c.name: store the operand in field 0x5f and run the note handler
0x1ae3c.why: an entry into the channel's note handler, which the driver reaches by tail jump; they share the same voice record in a2 and the same note and operand registers. This one writes byte 0x5f first.

0x1b06e.name: look the note up in the table at 0x1EA3C, or take the bend
0x1b06e.why: masks the caller's word to four bits, indexes 0x1EA3C, and a 0xFF entry means there is no note there and the word at +0x5A of the record - the bend - is used instead.

0x1b166.name: count the four sample voices down and retrigger the ones that expire
0x1b166.why: only every eighth call - the byte at 0x3E3D6C counts down from 7. For each of the four bits of the mask byte, decrements that voice's word in the pair table at 0x3E3D72 and, when it reaches zero, writes the voice's byte from 0x1EA94 to the OKI port and reloads the counter with 5.

0x1b2b2.name: start the sample for a channel by writing its number to the OKI
0x1b2b2.why: walks the four bytes at 0x3E3D6E, indexing the ten-byte records at 0x1B674 by each, and on the first whose field +1 matches the requested channel writes that slot's byte from 0x1EA94 straight to 0x460000 - the OKI6295's command port.

0x1b306.name: start a channel: clear its counters and run its script
0x1b306.why: zeroes 0x3E3706, 0x3E36FA and 0x3E36EC, then runs the channel's script through 0x1A5F0.

0x1b42e.name: select the instrument the channel's byte names
0x1b42e.why: indexes the six-byte records at 0x19CE4 by the byte and stores the long it finds in 0x3E36DA, which is the instrument pointer every note lookup then reads.

0x1b4be.name: strobe the input latch and write the YM's address
0x1b4be.why: clears bit 0 of the shadow at 0x3E3D8E, writes it to 0x640000, sets the bit and writes again - a strobe - then works on the YM2413 at 0x480000.

0x1b538.name: play one channel's next event on the YM
0x1b538.why: clears 0x3E3708, then works through the channel's counters at 0x3E3706 and 0x3E370A with the flag at 0x3E36EC, writing to the YM2413 at 0x480000.

0x1b612.name: start every other channel of the type's pair, up to nine
0x1b612.why: takes the type's field +5 from the six-byte records at 0x19CE4, points 0x3E36DE at 0x19CF0, and adds one to the index when bit 0 of 0x3E36D4 is set. Then it walks two at a time to nine, calling 0x1B538 on each with the list head from 0x3E3D12.

0x1e7b8.name: emit two decoded bytes a row at a time, biased by d2
0x1e7b8.why: the same two-byte loop as 0x12574, but each byte has d2 added - the colour base - and the row stride is the fixed 0x1F8 with a count of 7 rather than a stride in d5.

0x1e7e4.name: expand one nibble pair across an eight-by-eight block
0x1e7e4.why: the high nibble of d0 is the repeat count and the low nibble plus d2 the value, written down a column with the 0x1F8 row stride and a count of 7. 0x1E804 below it is a separate entry doing the same expansion in place, rewriting each byte's low nibble from the caller's word.

0x1e834.name: fill an eight-by-four block of the playfield with one byte
0x1e834.why: four `move.b d0,(a1)+` under a `dbra` on d1, then `lea $1fc(a1),a1` to the next row and d1 reloaded, eight rows in all. 0x1FC plus the four bytes just written is the 0x200 stride.

0x1e862.name: decompress a byte as two hexadecimal digits
0x1e862.why: splits the byte at (a3) into nibbles, turns each into 0x30..0x39 or 0x41.. by adding 7 past 0x3A, biases by 0x13 and hands it to decompressTileId with 0x1B - so each nibble becomes the tile of its own digit. Loops on d3, so it renders a whole number.

0x1e8d2.name: halt with every interrupt masked, upper image
0x1e8d2.why: `stop #$2700` in the upper half of the image, reached separately from the overlay's 0x62e and 0x642.

0x1e8d6.name: the crash screen: freeze the machine and print its registers
0x1e8d6.why: masks every interrupt, clears the watchdog, pushes all sixteen registers, copies eight bytes of palette from 0x1E85A to 0x3C03E0 so there is something visible, and renders the register dump as hexadecimal from 0x203030 through 0x1E8C8. It does not return.

0x1e9b4.name: restart through the reset vector
0x1e9b4.why: `suba.l a0,a0; movea.l (a0)+,a7; movea.l (a0),a0; jmp (a0)` - the same restart as 0x133a6 without masking interrupts first.

0x140010.name: board ROM zero stub
0x140010.why: moveq #0,d0 and rts, at the first address of the protection window. It is one of the two routines that cannot be compared against silicon, and the reason is recorded: that window is served by a state machine, so what the chip FETCHES there depends on the access sequence and differs from what reading the same address returns. The port answers zero, and difficultyClamp is its only caller.

0x1400e4.name: board ROM table compare
0x1400e4.why: the other half of the protection probe, and it is a comparison whose result is never stored: cmpm.w (a0)+,(a1)+ against 0x1432a0 and against 0x40148 plus the argument times 16, with dead tst instructions on 0x140000 and 0x1432b0 before each. Only the flags survive the rts, so the caller branches on Z. Like 0x140010 it is incomparable against the chip because the window is a state machine and fetching differs from reading.

0xef58.name: remove every posting of an event routine
0xef58.why: the fourth operation on the event list at 0x3e1cf4/0x3e1cf6 with its 0xc stride, and the one the old name `eventQueueAccess` could not distinguish from the other three. It matches on the routine pointer ALONE, like the test at 0xeffa and unlike the post at 0xee90 and the remove at 0xeeee, which both match the argument too - and having compacted one entry away it branches back to the top and scans again, so it removes ALL postings of that routine whatever arguments they were posted with.

0x1980.name: point each player's two cursor sprites at its marked cell
0x1980.why: walks the three player structs - lea 0x3e1968, adda 0x7e, three times - and for each takes the byte pair at 0x46 and 0x47, the cell coordinates 0x670e clears, shifts each left six and stores the word through the pointers at 0x5e and 0x62, which fields.txt records as the struct's two movea-loaded longs. So the two sprites follow the marked cell at 64 units to the cell. When the word argument is zero it calls 0x19d8 with the player instead, which is the reset side.

0x7a88.name: draw a number at a panel position, twice when told to
0x7a88.why: the word at 0xe(a6) selects where. When it is 1 the position comes from the table at 0x117ac and the same value is drawn a second time from 0x117aa - two fixed places, which is how this ROM draws a shadow under a figure; otherwise the position is the word at 0x3e1886. Either way the position word is stored at -2(a6) and its two BYTES are pushed separately as the coordinates, and the value at 0xa(a6) goes with a width of 2 and a mask of 0xf0 to the draw at 0x260. Nothing here reads a projectile or a speed, which is what the derived name claimed.

0x17500.name: clear the screen and the low work RAM, then reinitialise video
0x17500.why: clears 0x200000 to 0x220000 a long at a time - the whole 128 KiB playfield - then 0x3e0000 to 0x3e0800, the first 2 KiB of work RAM, writes 0xf0 to 0x3e366c and 0x1fc to 0x3e366a, and calls 0x19366. The derived name `recordWhetherVectorHoldsStubWrapper` describes the routine it happens to call and nothing this one does.

0x18b26.name: format the number into a local buffer, then draw it
0x18b26.why: a sixteen-byte buffer on its own frame at -0x10(a6): formatNumberPaddingSeparators fills it and the entry below draws from it.

0x14b2c.name: address of a sound channel's nth five-byte queue entry
0x14b2c.why: answers 0x3e3554 + channel * 50 + slot * 5, from the word at 0x16(a7) and the word at 0x12(a7): 50 is ten entries of five bytes, so the table is three channels of ten. It answers 0 for a channel of 3 or more and for a slot past ten - 10 - slot going negative is the test - and when the longword at 0x18(a7) is not null it writes how many slots remain after this one, times five, through it. That optional second answer is why it takes a pointer at all.

0x5b4.name: debounce one switch port and answer the bits that just changed
0x5b4.why: the word argument picks the port - 0x640002 for 0, 0x640000 for 1, 0x640001 otherwise - and the byte is immediately eor'd with the entry of the PC-relative table at 0x5b0 indexed by the same word, which is the per-port active-low mask. The state lives at 0x3e0836 + port: (a1) is the debounced level and 6(a1) the PREVIOUS raw sample, and a bit only moves the debounced level when the raw agrees with the previous one, which is a two-sample debounce. The byte at 0xf(a7) then selects which bits are reported and latched, and the answer is the changed bits within that mask.

0x156ac.name: roll a play-time accumulator into the bookkeeping counters
0x156ac.why: the longword table at 0x3e3632 indexed by kind * 4 is an accumulator that this routine drains and clears. On the way it adds the same amount into two more tables - 0x3e3652 indexed by the low bit of the second argument, and 0x3e3642 indexed by kind - and each of those, once past 0xe10, is divided by 0xe10, has the remainder written back, and passes the quotient to 0x14a36 under a category of 7, 8, 9 or higher by kind. The drained total is then divided by 0x1c20 for kind 3 and 0x708 otherwise, floored by 0 or 3, clamped to 0x13, and reported to 0x15064 under a code 0 to 4 chosen from the kind and the second argument. 0xe10, 0x708 and 0x1c20 are 3600, 1800 and 7200; the routine never says what the unit is, so neither does this.

0x1485c.name: write one packed bookkeeping counter and refresh its display
0x1485c.why: the write side of 0x14772 and provably the same store: the same 0x16 index limit, the same descriptor table at 0x1d616, and the same packed nibble array at 0x3e34cc. It also uses the descriptor's low five bits - `andi.l #$1f`, zero meaning none - to index the table at 0x3e34f4 and redraw through 0x143b0 into 0x3e3536, which is what makes the operator page update when a counter moves. The derived name `startSoundCue` is wrong.

0x14a36.name: add to a bookkeeping counter, and roll the coin display when it carries
0x14a36.why: reads the counter through 0x14772, adds the longword argument, and writes it back through 0x1485c, answering the new value; a read of -1 - the out-of-range answer - makes it return without writing. Counter 3 is special: when old xor new reaches 0x100 the count has crossed a byte boundary, and it then steps the byte at 0x3e34ed by 2, wrapping to 0x1a once it passes 0x21 above 0xff, and redraws two entries of the table at 0x3e34cc and three of 0x3e34f4 through 0x143b0. The derived name `soundChannelKey` is wrong.

0x143b0.name: queue an index and value for the consumer, or just mark it
0x143b0.why: a four-entry ring at 0x3e3508, eight bytes each - the longword argument at 0x20(a7) and the index word at 0x1c(a7) - with the write cursor at 0x3e3528 and the read cursor at 0x3e352a. Full is write+1 == read, and it SPINS there, clearing the watchdog at 0x72fffe and re-reading 0x12(a2) until something else moves the read cursor, so this routine blocks. Before enqueuing it consults the table at 0x1d64a, eight bytes an entry and terminated by a zero long at +4: a base word (0xff meaning take the base from 0x3e34ed), a count, and a key. An index inside a band whose key matches value - index*10 is NOT enqueued; instead bit (index & 7) of 0x3e352c + (index >> 3) is set, which is a bitmap of things already accounted for. It is called by the bookkeeping counter writer at 0x1485c with 0x3e3536, the counter and its new value. What drains the ring is not visible from here, and the entry this replaces called it a sound channel update on the strength of the address alone.

0x17fcc.name: substitute the stored default attributes, then measure the string
0x17fcc.why: two byte arguments with 0xff meaning 'use the stored default': 0xff in the second takes BOTH bytes from the pair at 0x3e3d7a and 0x3e3d7b, which 0x1357c initialises with move.b #$f,0x3e3d7b followed by copying it to 0x3e3d7a; 0xff in the first alone falls back to 0x2a. It then pushes the string pointer and calls 0x1868c, and its extent ends on that jsr - the branches to 0x18006 leave this routine and land in the next one, so it falls through rather than returning.

0x663c.name: reserve two bytes on the coordinate stack
0x663c.why: three instructions: it adds 2 to the pointer at 0x3e209c and answers the new value. It writes nothing THERE - every caller does that itself, and 0x5e38 is the pattern, taking the answer into a1 and copying its two coordinate bytes through it. So this reserves a slot rather than pushing a value, which is why the flood fill can hand the address straight to a byte copy.

0xee3a.name: empty the event list
0xee3a.why: one store: 0xffff into the word at 0x3e1cf4. That word is the event list's count held as count-minus-one, which is why the dispatcher at 0xee44 and both the post and the remove start with `bmi` - negative means none - so -1 is empty and this is the whole reset.

0x1e6b2.name: turn a cell x and y into a screen address, in place
0x1e6b2.why: takes the byte at 0x27(a7) as the row and the byte at 0x23(a7) as the column, and computes row << 12 plus column << 3 plus 0x200004 - the same address 0x11bec builds, because a cell is eight bytes wide and a row of cells is 0x1000, eight screen rows of 0x200. It then writes that address BACK over its own argument at 0x20(a7) and copies the word at 0x2a(a7) down to 0x26(a7), so it is a fixup of a parameter block rather than a function with an answer.

0xeac8.name: set or clear the selector byte, only in mode one
0xeac8.why: does nothing at all unless the byte at 0x3e1954 is exactly 1. In that mode it writes 0x3e195c from the ROM constant at 0x118aa when the byte at 0x3e1cb4 is non-zero, and clears it when that byte is zero. Three memory locations and no arguments; 0x3e195c is the byte 0xcae2 tests before it will fire.

0x12026.name: fill an eight by four block with one byte
0x12026.why: writes the low byte of the word at 0x16(a7) four times - dbra from 3 - then advances the pointer by 0x1fc and does it again, eight times over, dbra from 7. Four written plus 0x1fc is 0x200, the playfield row stride, so the block is four bytes wide and eight rows tall: half the width of the eight-byte cell the rest of the drawing code uses.

0x661a.name: pop two bytes off the coordinate stack into a fixed slot
0x661a.why: reads the two bytes at the top of the stack whose pointer is 0x3e209c into the fixed pair at 0x3e1f1a, drops the pointer by 2, and answers 0x3e1f1a. It is the exact inverse of 0x663c, which adds 2 and answers the new top for the caller to write through - so the pointer always points AT the last pair written, and the flood fill's 0xff empty marker is a value in the stack rather than a state of the pointer.

0xf2cc.name: follow two levels of the 0x1f7f0 offset table
0xf2cc.why: adds the word at the pointer it is given to 0x1f7f0 to get a second address, then adds the word THERE to 0x1f7f0 again and answers that. Both levels are 16-bit offsets from the same base, which is how this ROM stores a table of tables inside the first 128 KiB - the offsets stay words rather than longs.

0x5cb0.name: set the low four bits of a record's 0xc field and mark it for redraw
0x5cb0.why: reads the word at 0xc of the record, clears its low four bits with andi.w #$fff0, adds the word argument, and writes it back - so the argument is a 0..15 field packed into the bottom of that word and everything above it is preserved. It then ors 0x20 into the byte at offset 2, which is the same redraw bit 0xaf72 sets on a display entry after it moves one.

0x11ce2.name: write a three-byte entry as a word then its low byte again
0x11ce2.why: three bytes out of one longword argument: move.w writes the low WORD and the pointer advances two, then move.b writes the low BYTE again at the third position. So the entry reads [byte 2][byte 3][byte 3] - the last component is a repeat of the one before it, not a third value out of the argument, and a caller packing three separate things into that longword would be wrong.

0x130ee.name: re-enter the self test with the power-on flag clear
0x130ee.why: three instructions: mask every interrupt with sr = 0x2700, clear d3, and branch to 0x135ba, which is INSIDE 0x1357c - one instruction past the moveq #$1,d3 that the power-on path runs. So d3 is what tells the self test apart from itself: 1 when the board just came up, 0 when the operator asked for it from the menu, and 0x1378e reads it to decide whether to run the long RAM passes.

0x13f40.name: load the packed options word from bookkeeping counter 20 and cache it
0x13f40.why: reads counter 0x14 through 0x14772 - the packed-nibble bookkeeping store - and, unless the read came back negative, keeps it as a WORD at 0x3e3444 and sets the byte at 0x3e344a to 1. That byte is the 'have we loaded it' flag every accessor tests first, and 0x3e3444 is the packed settings word the accessors at 0x13f60 and 0x13f98 pull fields out of.

0x13f60.name: read the three-bit option at bits 11 to 13, if bit 14 enables it
0x13f60.why: answers 0xff when the cache flag at 0x3e344a is clear - not loaded, rather than a value of 255 - and 0 when bit 0x4000 of the cached word at 0x3e3444 is clear, which is the enable. Otherwise it takes (word >> 11) & 7 and answers (n + 2) >> 1, so the three raw bits 0..7 become 1,1,2,2,3,3,4,4. 0x13f98 next door is the same shape reading a different field behind bit 0x8000.

0x1418a.name: is this count still within the allowance
0x1418a.why: answers 0xff when the options word has not been loaded - the byte at 0x3e344a - and 1 when the option that 0x13f98 reads is off, which is the 'no limit' case. Otherwise it adds the two bytes at 0x3e3446 and 0x3e3448 and answers 1 while that sum is at or above the longword argument, 0 once the argument passes it. So 1 means allowed and 0 means refused, and the two bytes are the allowance.

0x15858.name: count one more of bookkeeping counter 13
0x15858.why: five instructions: push 1, push 0xd, call the counter adder at 0x14a36, drop the arguments. Nothing else. It is a named place to add one to counter 13, which is why it has its own six-byte stub at 0x278.

0x8fc8.name: find a pair in the 0x3e1900 table and mark it taken
0x8fc8.why: walks two-byte entries at 0x3e1900 until the first byte goes negative, which is the terminator, comparing each against the pair the caller passed. On a match it writes 0xff into the SECOND byte of that entry and answers 1; running off the end answers 0. The caller's pair is copied a byte at a time into a local before being read as a word, which is the lifter-visible form of reading a word that may sit at an odd address.

0x125da.name: tick the head of the 0x3e20a0 timer list and dispatch it
0x125da.why: does nothing while the byte at 0x3e2498 is set, which is the pause. The list at 0x3e20a0 is circular and empty when the head points at itself - `cmpa.l a0,a1; beq` is the whole emptiness test. It counts the byte at 0xe of the first record down, and only when it reaches zero reloads it from 0xd - so 0xd is the period and 0xe the remainder - takes the pointer at 8 into a2, and jumps through a PC-relative word table at 0x1261a indexed by the kind byte at 0xc times two.

0x7c72.name: start the phase: post two events, arm two flags
0x7c72.why: posts 0x11b30 with an argument of 1 and 0x11b1e with 0 through 0xee90, writes 0xfe to 0x3e0dc4 and 1 to 0x3e0ebe, and hands the longword at 0x117b6 to 0x53a6. Five side effects and no answer - it is the opening of a phase rather than anything that decides. The derived name says a countdown beep and nothing here reaches a sound chip.

0xc5ca.name: schedule a palette fade to an explicit IRGB colour
0xc5ca.why: kind ZERO - clr.b 0xc(a2) - and the one that takes a colour apart rather than a packed word. Four byte arguments are masked and shifted into four separate words in the record: & 1 << 15 at 0x10, & 0x1f << 10 at 0x12, & 0x1f << 5 at 0x14, and & 0x1f at 0x16. That is exactly the IRGB 1-5-5-5 the port's own palette decode in system.ts reassembles - intensity, red, green, blue - so the record holds the target colour as components, which is what lets the tick ramp each of them separately. The address at 0x8 and the link into 0x3e20a0 are the same as the rest of the family.

0x35ee.name: walk a rectangle with the per-cell routine at 0x11eda
0x35ee.why: sixty bytes, and every one of them is argument shuffling: it reorders its five arguments and pushes 0x11eda in front of them for the higher-order walk at 0x357a. 0x35ee and 0x3666 are the same instructions with a different per-cell routine, which is the entire difference between them. A trap in reading it: the two `move.w $1e(a7),d0` are NOT the same slot - a7 has dropped four bytes between them, so the first reads the argument at off 20 and the second the one at off 16.

0x3666.name: walk a rectangle with the per-cell routine at 0x11ee6
0x3666.why: sixty bytes, and every one of them is argument shuffling: it reorders its five arguments and pushes 0x11ee6 in front of them for the higher-order walk at 0x357a. 0x35ee and 0x3666 are the same instructions with a different per-cell routine, which is the entire difference between them. A trap in reading it: the two `move.w $1e(a7),d0` are NOT the same slot - a7 has dropped four bytes between them, so the first reads the argument at off 20 and the second the one at off 16.

0x362a.name: walk a rectangle with the per-cell routine at 0x11efe
0x362a.why: the third of an identical set - 0x35ee pushes 0x11eda, 0x3666 pushes 0x11ee6 and this one 0x11efe - in front of the higher-order walk at 0x357a. Sixty bytes each and the same instructions, so the per-cell routine is the whole content of the choice. 0x11efe has thirteen callers of its own and decompresses one eight-pixel column, which is what makes this the ordinary path for drawing a rectangle of them.

0x36a2.name: walk a rectangle with a per-cell attribute byte alongside
0x36a2.why: 0x357a's shape with the per-cell routine fixed at 0x11eda and one thing added: a SECOND stream. Each cell takes a word from the list at 8(a6) and a BYTE from the pointer at 0x18(a6), and the attribute handed to 0x11eda is that byte shifted left four plus the base word from 0x1e(a6). The byte pointer is advanced with `addq.l #$1,$18(a6)` - in the caller's own stack slot, not in a register - so the caller sees it moved on return, and that is also why it is absent from the params table: the lifter cannot bind a slot the routine writes.

0x46e0.name: register five graphic tables in five slots
0x46e0.why: one routine address held in a2 and called five times with an address and a slot number: 0x1f040 into 8, 0x1f060 into 9, 0x1f080 into 0xa, 0x1f0a0 into 0xb, and 0x1ef00 into 0xf. The first four are 0x20 apart, which is what makes them one table of four; the fifth is somewhere else entirely and goes in a slot six higher.

0x6648.name: lay the board out from a nibble-per-cell stream
0x6648.why: walks the board at 0x3e0864 against the screen at 0x200004, taking a byte from the caller's stream and masking it to its low four bits for each cell. A nibble of 6 or less indexes a PC-relative jump table at 0x66ba, seven ways; anything higher takes the default. The bounds it tests are 0x29 and 0x1d - 41 and 29, one less than the 42 by 30 the piece walker at 0x8b4 bounds against - so the first and last row and column are handled as edges and take the default rather than reading a nibble.

0xc9d2.name: schedule a palette effect of kind seven
0xc9d2.why: instruction for instruction the same routine as 0xc8de - allocate through 0xc504, palette address 0x3c0000 + bank * 64 + page * 0x400, value at 0x10, period at 0xd, delay PLUS ONE at 0xe, 0xf set to 1, and the link into 0x3e20a0 with 0x3e2498 held across it - differing only in the kind byte, which is 7 here and 2 there. The derived name `helperFramebufferBandClearInner` describes neither the framebuffer nor a band: it touches nothing but palette RAM and the timer list.

0x11efe.name: decompress one eight-pixel column and answer the next address
0x11efe.why: sets d4 to 7 - the eight rows the decoder at 0x11f2a counts down - clears d3, points a0 at 0xd2608 plus the caller's word offset, and falls into that decoder. The answer is the destination PLUS EIGHT, which is exactly the contract the higher-order walk at 0x357a needs from a per-cell routine: take the address, draw, hand back where the next cell starts. 0xd2608 is where the compressed graphics live.

0x19c00.name: fill bytes, with a full 32-bit count
0x19c00.why: writes the byte at 8(a7) count-plus-one times - dbra counts to -1, so the argument is one less than the length - and gets past 65535 with `subi.l #$10000,d0; bcc`, which runs the dbra again for each whole 64K. It answers the address it started at, not the address it finished at.

0xe332.name: set up the high-score entry: three A's, a random prompt, a 1200-tick clock
0xe332.why: picks one of EIGHT strings from the longword table at 0x11a50 - `pea 8` to the RNG at 0x11e58, whose answer is scaled into 0..7 rather than masked - and keeps the pointer at 0x3e1cdc. It fills three bytes at 0x3e1cd8 with 0x41, which is 'A', so the initials start at AAA; copies the chosen string's first byte to 0x3e1cd6 and clears the two bytes after it; and sets 0x3e1cd2 to 0x4b0, which is 1200 - twenty seconds at sixty ticks. The draw at the end takes 0x12, 0x19, the buffer and 0xf0.

0x1512.name: call one routine per set bit of the 0x3e0dc8 flag word
0x1512.why: shifts the word at 0x3e0dc8 left one bit at a time, fifteen times, and calls the routine at the matching entry of the longword table at 0xfcf2 whenever the bit that fell off the top was set - `bge` skipping the call, so it is testing the sign after the shift. Bit 15 goes first, so the table is in most-significant-bit order. After that it calls 0x128bc only when all four of 0x3e195c above 4, 0x3e1956 zero, 0x3e1948 exactly 0x11 and 0x3e1cc8 non-zero hold at once.

0x5e02.name: answer the argument unchanged
0x5e02.why: two instructions - `move.l $4(a7),d0` and `rts` - so it is the identity function on its first argument. There are at least two of these in the image, 0x5e02 and 0xdb66, each called from one place (currentPieceDraw here), which is what a compiler leaves behind when a call that used to do something has had its body removed rather than its call sites.

0xdb66.name: answer the argument unchanged
0xdb66.why: two instructions - `move.l $4(a7),d0` and `rts` - so it is the identity function on its first argument. There are at least two of these in the image, 0x5e02 and 0xdb66, each called from one place (playerFlagHandler here), which is what a compiler leaves behind when a call that used to do something has had its body removed rather than its call sites.

0xdb78.name: answer the argument unchanged
0xdb78.why: `move.l $4(a7),d0` then `rts`, the third of these in the image after 0x5e02 and 0xdb66, called from fireTrigger. Two instructions and no effect.

0x5dea.name: do nothing
0x5dea.why: one instruction, `rts`. It is reached from mainLoop and there is nothing else to say about it - which is worth saying, because a routine with a caller and no body is the shape a reader stops and re-reads.

0x5dfe.name: do nothing
0x5dfe.why: one instruction, `rts`. It is reached from mainGameStateMachine and there is nothing else to say about it - which is worth saying, because a routine with a caller and no body is the shape a reader stops and re-reads.

0x3ea.name: kick the watchdog, then stamp a fixed block and clear two words
0x3ea.why: calls the watchdog kick at 0x618 and then writes a fixed pattern nobody computes: the words 9, 0xd, 0xa, 0xe into 0x3e3f00 onwards, then 0x5b95, 0x1016 and 0xb087 into 0x3e3f08, 0x3e3f0a and 0x3e3f0c. All seven are constants in the instruction stream, so this is a signature or a seed rather than anything derived. It then clears the words at 0x3e0802 and 0x3e0800 and reads each back, which is the shape of a write-then-verify on hardware rather than of a variable being reset.

0x5608.name: count a byte down and remove the event when it reaches zero
0x5608.why: an inner entry that arrives with a3 pointing at the counter byte and a1 at the event argument - it takes neither from the stack. `subq.b #$1,(a3); bne` skips everything when the byte is still positive, and on the tick it reaches zero it removes 0x11bc6 through 0xeeee. So the byte is a repeat count and the event unhooks itself when it runs out.

0x16d3e.name: reset with argument one, then the shared tail at 0x16fe0
0x16d3e.why: pushes 1, calls 0x160ba, drops the argument and branches to 0x16fe0. Its middle - 0x16d48, the `addq.l #$4,a7` - is where 0x16d4e lands, so the argument drop and the branch are SHARED between the two: 0x16d4e's own path leaves a longword on the stack for this tail to remove.

0x16d4e.name: audio and video reset, then 0x1684c with 0x1e59c
0x16d4e.why: calls 0x181a4, pushes 0x1e59c and calls 0x1684c, then branches into the MIDDLE of 0x16d3e at 0x16d48, which drops that argument and goes on to the shared exit at 0x16fe0. Three routines - this, 0x16d3e and 0x16d60 - all end at 0x16fe0, and they differ only in which reset they call on the way.

0x16d60.name: audio and video reset, then 0x168f8
0x16d60.why: calls 0x181a4 then 0x168f8 and branches straight to 0x16fe0, taking no argument and leaving nothing on the stack - which is why it goes to the shared exit directly where 0x16d4e has to go through the drop at 0x16d48 first. The variant of the three that differs is 0x16d3e, which calls 0x160ba instead of 0x181a4.

0x16d6e.name: render the title screen, then the shared exit at 0x16fe0
0x16d6e.why: two instructions: call 0x1520e and branch to 0x16fe0. It is the fourth of the group that all end at 0x16fe0 - with 0x16d3e, 0x16d4e and 0x16d60 - and the one that leaves nothing on the stack, so it takes the exit directly.

0x193da.name: wait for the counter at 0x3e3404 to change, n plus one times
0x193da.why: reads the word at 0x3e3404 into d1 and then spins on `cmp.w (a0),d1; beq` until it differs - so it waits for something OUTSIDE this program to move that word, which is what makes it a hardware counter rather than a variable. The dbra around it runs the wait once more than the argument says. There is no timeout and no watchdog kick inside the spin.

0x18e00.name: claim a slot with kind three
0x18e00.why: the same two instructions with a three.

0x18db6.name: claim a slot as kind five or six, by the sign of the argument
0x18db6.why: another head on the body at 0x18e06 that 0x18e00 also falls into. It picks the kind from the SIGN of the word argument - 6 when positive, and 5 after negating it when not - so one argument carries both a magnitude and a choice of kind. 0x18dc4 is a third head on the same body, using kind 7 and setting 0x3e340a and 0x3e3406 first.

0x193c6.name: write one word into the playfield by word index
0x193c6.why: `adda.l d0,a0` twice rather than a shift, which is the compiler's way of doubling without touching the flags, so the argument is a WORD index and not a byte offset - the address is 0x200000 + index * 2. It writes the word at 0xa(a7) there and returns. Note the base is 0x200000, four bytes below the 0x200004 every drawing routine uses.

0x141c4.name: clear both allowance bytes
0x141c4.why: three instructions: zero into 0x3e3447 and 0x3e3446. Those are the pair that 0x1418a adds together to decide whether a count is still within the allowance, so this is the reset of that budget - and it clears 0x3e3447 as well, which 0x1418a does not read, so the two bytes are not simply a two-digit number.

0x14104.name: draw the allowance down until it is under a whole unit
0x14104.why: answers 0xff when the options word has not been loaded, and 1 immediately when the option 0x13f98 reads is zero - which is the same 'no limit' answer 0x1418a gives. Otherwise it calls 0x14044 and, while that answers 0x10000 or more, subtracts the option value from 0x3e3448 and asks again, answering 0 once it drops below. So the loop spends the allowance a unit at a time rather than dividing.

0x14230.name: divide the counter read by 0x141d4 by the option value
0x14230.why: the same two guards as its neighbours - 0xff when the options word is not loaded, 0 when the option 0x13f98 reads is zero - and then it pushes that option, calls 0x141d4 to read counter 2 through 0x14772, and hands both to the divide at 0x1869e. The zero guard is what stops the divide from being by zero, which is worth seeing before anyone rearranges it.

0x14b8a.name: unpack a channel queue entry into its three-byte and two-byte fields
0x14b8a.why: asks 0x14b2c for the address of one five-byte entry - slot first, channel second, and a null third argument because it does not want the remaining count - and answers 0 when that comes back null. It then reassembles bytes 0, 1 and 2 into a 24-bit value at 0x3e344c and bytes 3 and 4 into a 16-bit one, which is what the five bytes are: three plus two, not five separate things.

0x14d48.name: write a 24-bit value into a channel's queue
0x14d48.why: the inverse of 0x14b8a and it uses the same 0x14b2c, but with slot ZERO and a real pointer for the remaining count - so it always writes at the head and wants to know how much room is left. It refuses anything above 0xffffff, which confirms the entry's first field is 24 bits wide and not a longword.

0x3726.name: do nothing
0x3726.why: one instruction, `rts`. The third and fourth of these found by reading; there are thirteen routines in the image whose whole body is a return, and the note exists so a reader does not go looking for the rest of one.

0x5e00.name: do nothing
0x5e00.why: one instruction, `rts`. The third and fourth of these found by reading; there are thirteen routines in the image whose whole body is a return, and the note exists so a reader does not go looking for the rest of one.

0xd030.name: enter the next phase: zero the countdown, set the state byte to two
0xd030.why: calls 0x1a8 with a zero argument and 0xd490 with one, clears the byte at 0x3e1870 - the phase countdown that 0x7a24 decrements and 0xcae2 tests - writes 2 through a2, and branches on to 0xd45c rather than returning. Five side effects and a tail branch, so it is a transition and not a query. a2 arrives from the caller, which is why the state byte it writes is not visible here.

0x9188.name: the reset sequence: eleven calls in a fixed order
0x9188.why: no branches, no arguments and no answer - eleven `jsr`s one after another: 0x5cce, the watchdog kick at 0x618, 0x160, the event-list reset at 0xee3a, 0xc568, 0x23c, 0xfbe4, the watchdog again, 0x620, 0x17e and 0x1fa. The watchdog appears twice inside the list, which says the calls between them take long enough to matter. The order is the whole content of the routine.

0x1310c.name: clear from 0x200000 to 0x3e07fe, kicking the watchdog every 1024 words
0x1310c.why: one huge wipe - `clr.w (a0)+` from 0x200000 until a0 reaches 0x3e07fe, which is the playfield, everything above it and the low work RAM together. The dbeq counts 0x3ff at a time and the exit test is `cmpa.l a0,a1`, so on each thousand-word block that does NOT reach the end it writes 0x72fffe and starts another: the watchdog would trip long before a wipe that size finished otherwise. It leaves by `jmp $300`, not by returning.

0x5e08.name: do nothing
0x5e08.why: one instruction, `rts`, and nothing else in its extent.

0xa7e4.name: do nothing
0xa7e4.why: one instruction, `rts`, and nothing else in its extent.

0xfc0e.name: do nothing
0xfc0e.why: one instruction, `rts`, and nothing else in its extent.

0xfc44.name: do nothing
0xfc44.why: one instruction, `rts`, and nothing else in its extent.

0x66cc.name: re-enter the board walk at its default-cell path
0x66cc.why: NOT a do-nothing, whatever the derived name says: its two bytes are `bra.b $669c`, which lands inside 0x6648 - the routine that lays the board out from a nibble-per-cell stream - at the point that takes the default for a cell instead of reading a nibble. So it is an inner entry that says 'this cell is an edge', reached by a jump table rather than by a call, and a reader who trusts the name will look for a body that is not there.

0x13e94.name: count the coin slots that fired and take the credits
0x13e94.why: the two counters live at 0x3e3444 and 0x3e3447, and the whole routine is skipped when the byte at 0x3e344a is clear - the same gate the tick accumulator uses.

0xfc9a.name: do nothing
0xfc9a.why: one instruction, `rts`, and nothing else in its extent.

0x1228a.name: do nothing
0x1228a.why: one instruction, `rts`, and nothing else in its extent.

0x1232c.name: do nothing
0x1232c.why: one instruction, `rts`, and nothing else in its extent.

0x43a.name: check that movem round-trips d0 to d3, rotating the pattern
0x43a.why: an inner entry of 0x430 that starts the test at a different seed - d0 already holds 0xaaaaaaaa here where the head at 0x430 sets it to 0x55555555 - and otherwise loads d1 to d3 with 0xaaaaaaaa, 0xff and 0, pushes all four with `movem.l d0-d3`, and compares each against the copy on the stack - any mismatch calls 0x3e8 with 0x3ab, which is the failure report. On a pass it ROTATES the four values, d0 taking d1's and so on round, and goes again, so every value visits every register. The loop runs until the word at 0x3e0802 counts down, and that word is also clamped to 4 afterwards. It is a self test of the instruction the whole lifted world depends on for saving registers across an interrupt.

0xd9a2.name: step the player's rotation cursor unless its event is still pending
0xd9a2.why: asks 0xeffa whether 0x11b1e is scheduled - the test that matches on the routine alone rather than on routine and argument - and does nothing at all if it is. Otherwise it steps the cursor at 0x24(a2) through 0x5afc, but only while 0x24 and 0x2c differ, so 0x2c is where the ring started. It then makes this player current by writing a2 to 0x3e1960 and calls 0x5192; and if the cursor has come back round to 0x2c it removes 0x11b96. So one event gates the stepping and another is retired when the rotation has been all the way round.

0x1997c.name: store d3 into 0x12 of the record and branch on its sign
0x1997c.why: an inner entry of 0x1997a that arrives with d3 and a2 already set: it writes the word and takes `bpl` on the flags THAT WRITE left, not on a separate test. A reader looking for the comparison will not find one - `move.w` sets N and Z from the value moved, which is the whole reason this is two instructions rather than three.

0x1a8c0.name: assemble the sixteen bit word at field 0x1a
0x1a8c0.why: the operand is its low byte and 0x1a8d4 fetches the next script byte for the high one, advancing 4(a2) past it. setChannelSPitchNote subtracts that word from the channel's 32-bit accumulator at 0xa every tick, so it is a per-tick slide step.

0x1822c.name: draw a block of text lines at consecutive rows
0x1822c.why: the same four-argument shape over and over - attribute 0x2000, a string, a row and a kind - alternating between 0x17fcc, which substitutes the stored default attributes when 0xff is passed, and 0x13e6a. The row is the word argument for the first line and that plus one for the next, so the block runs down the screen from wherever the caller says. 0x2000 is the same attribute for every line.

0xebc4.name: redraw the whole board and the player's panel
0xebc4.why: sets two bytes at 0x3e1cec to 1 and clears the four after them, then calls the rectangle walk at 0x362a with width 0x2a and height 0x1e - 42 by 30, the board's full size, confirmed here for the third time after 0x8b4's bounds and 0x6648's edge tests - starting at 0x200004 with an extra of 0xb0. The cell list comes from the longword table at 0x215ce indexed by the byte at 0x3e0dd4, so that byte chooses which board is drawn. It then draws the player's own pieces through 0xecb0 from the pointer at 0x4a(a2).

0x441c.name: draw a two-by-two marker at the player's 0x3c coordinate
0x441c.why: copies the byte PAIR at 0x3c(a2) into a local and hands it to 0x11bec as one word - so 0x3c and 0x3d are a packed coordinate, the same shape the cell and screen address routines take. The colour comes from the byte table at 0xfe02 indexed by the player's own byte at 2(a2) PLUS ONE, and the size arguments are 2 and 2. It is called from the territory scoring at 0x865e, which is what makes this the mark that goes down when a region is claimed.

0x3c44.name: score one cell into the running total
0x3c44.why: hands a3, d2 and d4 to 0x3da0 and uses the answer to index the BYTE table at 0xfd96, adding what it finds to d5 - so d5 is a running total and the table is the value of whatever 0x3da0 identified. It then compares d3 against the 0xc0 owner bits of the cell byte at (a2), which is the same mask the piece walker and the flood fill use to ask whose a cell is. The arguments arrive in registers from the caller's loop rather than on the stack, which is why this is an inner step and not a routine anyone calls.

0x47c6.name: register seven of one table and a run of another
0x47c6.why: two loops through the same registrar 0x450c that 0x46e0 uses. The first puts 0xfdc2 into slots 0 to 6 - seven of them, `cmp.l d2,d4; ble` with d2 at 6. The second walks 0x1f6d0 in steps of 0x20 - `asl.l #$4` then `add.l d1,d1`, which is times sixteen then doubled - registering each into slot 8 with a third argument that counts up. So one table is seven separate registrations and the other is a run of equally spaced entries.

0x198c0.name: step one sequence record, flushing any pending byte first
0x198c0.why: the record's fields come out of what it does with them: 8(a2) is a pending write and 0x10(a2) its argument - when 8 is set it calls 0x19a24 and stores the answering byte through the pointer at 0xc(a2), then clears 8 so it happens once. 0(a2) is the sequence pointer, 4(a2) an index into it, 0x12(a2) a state and 0x16(a2) the value being matched. The state indexes the PC-relative BYTE table at 0x1996a - the twelve bytes that census work reclassified from a routine to data - and that byte, doubled, offsets the index before the comparison.

0x16d88.name: draw the self-test results page
0x16d88.why: a page laid out by hand: 0x174a2 first, then the block of lines at row 0x19 through 0x1822c, then two lines at rows 0x16 and 0x17 with attribute 0x2010 and the strings at 0x1dcd4 and 0x1dcf4. Those two are drawn through `jsr (a3)` with 0xffff as the first argument - and 0xffff is the marker 0x17fcc reads as 'use the stored default attributes', so the caller is asking for the defaults rather than passing a real value. It then takes the result of 0x130f8 into d4 and draws different things depending on whether it was zero.

0x162d6.name: check a value through two tests, then draw a row that depends on a ROM byte
