0x162d6.why: hands its first argument and the word at 0x26(a7) to 0x160f8, passes THAT answer to 0x160dc, and does nothing further when the second answers zero - so the two are a conversion followed by a validity test on the converted value, not two independent checks. The row it then draws at is 0x18 or 0x12 depending on the byte at 0x372, which is inside the exception vector table and so is a build-time constant rather than state - two fixed layouts chosen once.

0x13d1e.name: reduce a packed count into calendar-shaped components
0x13d1e.why: the constants say what it is doing even though the routine names nothing. It splits the low TWO bits off the argument, divides what is left by 0x5460 - 21,600 - and rotates those two bits back into the top of the value it writes to its own argument slot, which is the standard way of carrying a phase alongside a reduced count. It then adds 0x2db, 731, and divides by 0x5b5, 1461: 1461 is four years of 365.25 days and 731 is two of them plus one, which is the Julian day-to-year reduction. So the packed value is a time and the two bits are its quarter.

0x1997a.name: count the sequence step down and advance when it runs out
0x1997a.why: `subq.w #$1,d3` then storing d3 into 0x12(a2) and taking `bpl` on the flags that STORE left - no separate test - so 0x12 is a countdown and everything below happens only on the tick it goes negative. Then it clears the sequence pointer at 0(a2), copies 4(a3) into 7(a2), and asks 0x1425c whether to carry on. The new index at 4(a2) is the old one multiplied by (5(a3) + 5) and then doubled, so the stride comes out of the descriptor a3 points at rather than being fixed.

0x430.name: check movem round-trips d0 to d3, then sample the six input ports
0x430.why: seeds d0 to d3 with 0x55555555, 0xaaaaaaaa, 0xff and 0 and runs the same push-compare-rotate loop as its inner entry 0x43a, which differs only in starting d0 at 0xaaaaaaaa instead - so the two heads run the test with different patterns. Afterwards, and only when the word at 0x3e1948 is non-zero, it reads SIX ports at 0x6c0007, 0x6c0005, 0x6c0003, 0x6c0001, 0x6c0002 and 0x6c0000 - note the order, high to low and then the two even ones - into 0x3e0806, 0x3e080e, 0x3e0816, 0x3e081e, 0x3e0826 and 0x3e082e, eight bytes apart. So 0x6c0000 is the input block and each port gets an eight-byte record in work RAM.

0x1b1d2.name: start a sample, unless one of higher priority is playing
0x1b1d2.why: the argument is multiplied by TEN - doubled, then that times five - to index the table at 0x1b674, so the descriptors are ten bytes each. The byte at 2 of the chosen one is compared against 0x3e36e8 and `bcs` leaves without doing anything when it is lower, which makes 2 a priority and 0x3e36e8 what is currently playing. It then works through 0x460000 - the ADPCM chip, one of the two sound devices this port sees and ignores - with a byte from 0x1ea90 indexed by the descriptor's byte at 6.

0xa80c.name: clear the entity, marker and unit tables
0xa80c.why: three sized wipes, and the sizes are the useful part: sixteen records of 14 bytes from 0x3e1ae6 - dbra from 0xf with `lea $e(a0),a0` - then 32 BYTES at stride two from 0x3e1c44 all set to 0xff, and then seven records from 0x3e1bc6, which is the unit array 0xaf72 walks with the same count and the same 0x12 stride. So the three table geometries agree with what the routines that use them do, read from the other end. It calls 0xeac8 first, which does nothing unless the mode byte is 1.

0x169c8.name: draw the screen test pattern in sixteen-step bands
0x169c8.why: holds two routine addresses PC-relative in a2 and a3 - 0x1829c and 0x16958 - and then calls a2 over and over with a first argument that climbs 0, 0x10, 0x20, 0x30 and on, written out longhand rather than looped. Before that it clears the screen and reinitialises video through 0x17500 and sets d2 to 0x8000. Sixteen-step bands drawn one call at a time is a test pattern, and the unrolling is why it is 304 bytes.

0x40d2.name: draw a sprite through the per-cell attribute map
0x40d2.why: its first two BYTES are a coordinate pair - the byte at 9(a6) less one times 80, and the byte at 8(a6) less one doubled, added to the longword at 0x3e0e7a - so the map it indexes has an 80-byte row and two bytes a column, which is 40 columns and not the 42 the board uses. It takes the screen address for the same pair from 0x11bec, and walks with 0x28 - 40 - as the row limit. So this draws against the 40-column attribute map rather than against the 42-column board, and the two are not the same grid.

0xa20.name: resolve a shape's cells against a base and test the placement
0xa20.why: reads a byte stream whose pairs are row then column: the first is shifted left FIVE - the board's 32-byte row - and added to the base longword the caller passes, and the second added on top. So it walks the same board geometry the piece walker at 0x8b4 and the cell address at 0x11bd8 use, but against a base the caller chooses rather than 0x3e0864, which is what lets a placement be tried somewhere other than where it currently is. It keeps 0xfcca - the per-direction delta table - in a local, and reads the current player's byte at 2 through the pointer at 0x3e1960.

0xd916.name: choose the piece's rotation ring for this player
0xd916.why: does nothing when the byte at 0x3e194c is 0xe. Otherwise the player's byte at 2 indexes the longword table at 0x3e1cb8 for a descriptor, and THAT descriptor's byte at 2, times four, indexes 0xff90 for a longword written into 0x24(a2). 0x24 is the rotation cursor - 0xd9a2 steps it through 0x5afc and stops when it comes back to 0x2c - so 0xff90 is the table of rotation rings and this is what points a player at one. The descriptor's byte at 3 is read the same way for the field after it.

0x200a.name: answer which player, from the stored one or by scanning the three
0x200a.why: mode 2 reads the byte at 0x3e1ae2 and, when it is NEGATIVE, falls back to 0x3e0dce instead. 0x3e1ae2 is the byte 0x15b4 sets to 0xff, and 0x3e1968 + 3 * 0x7e is that same address - one past the third player's struct - so 0xff there means 'nobody chosen' and the sign test is how that is asked. Any other mode walks the three players at 0x3e1968 instead. It also keeps 0x3e1954, the mode byte 0xeac8 refuses to act on unless it is 1, in a local throughout.

0x6420.name: write a cell's low six bits and notify when the one after it reads two
0x6420.why: an inner step that arrives with its registers already set - d4 is the cell address, d2 the value and d5 the bits to or in, and it advances d4 itself. It masks the value to 0x3f before or-ing d5, so the top two bits are the owner field the whole board code reserves and the bottom six are the cell's own kind. It then looks at the byte 0x21 further on - one row plus one, on the 32-byte board - and only when THAT byte's low six bits are exactly 2 does it call the gate at 0x90e6, once, guarded by the counter at 0x14(a2) so a run of them notifies a single time.

0x3de8.name: answer which of the cells above and below carries either value
0x3de8.why: adds 1 to the cell address, looks 0x20 further on - one row down, on the 32-byte board - and adds 4 to the answer if that byte equals EITHER of the two the caller passed; then steps back 0x20 from there and adds 8 on the same test. So the answer is a two-bit mask, bit 2 for one neighbour and bit 3 for the other, and each is set by a match against either value rather than both. It is the same shape as the wall adjacency rule that `RULES.wallsConnectUp` switches - one bit per vertical neighbour, added rather than or-ed - though it is a different routine.

0x24c8.name: compare a cell's owner with the two vertically adjacent ones
0x24c8.why: masks the cell byte with 0xc0 - the owner field the whole board code reserves - and compares it against the same field of the cell 0x20 further on and the one 0x20 back, which is one board row either way. So it asks whether a cell has the same owner above and below it, where 0x3de8 next door asks whether the neighbours carry either of two whole values. Two different questions about the same two cells.

0x1865e.name: save the register file and the return address, and answer zero
0x1865e.why: five instructions and it is a setjmp. `movem.l d1-d7/a2-a7,(a0)` writes the whole register file into the caller's buffer, but d1 has first been replaced by the longword at (a7) - the RETURN ADDRESS - so the buffer holds where to come back to as well as what to come back with. It then answers 0, which is the other half of the convention: whatever restores this buffer answers something else, and the caller tells the two apart by the answer.

0x14eca.name: look one byte out of the six-by-twenty table at 0x3e3454
0x14eca.why: refuses a first argument of 6 or more and a second of 0x14 or more, answering 0xff - so the table is six rows of twenty and 0xff means out of range rather than a value. The first is multiplied by 0x14 and the second indexes within that row, which is what makes it row-major.

0x3da0.name: count how many of the three neighbours carry either value
0x3da0.why: 0x3de8's shape with a different answer: where that one adds 4 and 8 to make a two-bit mask, this adds ONE per match, so it answers a COUNT and not a set. Same three neighbours - the cell less one, that plus 0x20, and back again - and the same pair of acceptable values, either of which counts.

0x3194.name: draw the rubble tile at a coordinate
0x3194.why: ten instructions: turn the coordinate into a screen address with 0x11bec, then call the per-column decompressor 0x11efe with the WORD at 0x21c04 as the graphic offset and 0x10 as the palette base. The offset is read from memory rather than being a constant, so which graphic counts as rubble can be changed at run time. 0x8606 calls it right after writing 0x30 into a cell, which is what makes 0x30 the rubble value.

0x18b76.name: turn two byte coordinates into a screen address and draw the text
0x18b76.why: the row byte is swapped and shifted down four - the 0x1000 step a cell-row takes - and the column byte shifted left three, eight pixels a cell.

0x1851c.name: merge masked bits into the accumulated result
0x1851c.why: two longwords at 0x3e3d82 and 0x3e3d86 and a mask. It eors them, keeps only the bits the mask selects, ors those into 0x3e3d86, and rebuilds its answer as the unmasked part of the first plus the masked difference. So 0x3e3d86 accumulates every bit that has ever DIFFERED under a mask - which is what a self test wants: not the last result but every failure seen so far. A zero mask leaves both alone.

0x90be.name: queue a cue byte in the ring
0x90be.why: it writes the byte into 0x3e1922 at the head held in 0x3e1942, then advances the head and wraps it at 0x1f - a 32-entry circular queue push. It was called creditAdd, which is the same wrong reading baseline.json already records for 0x9080's creditCompare, and 0x9080 is the drain of this very ring.

0x1869e.name: divide two packed numerators by one divisor
0x1869e.why: two `divu.w` against the SAME divisor at 0xa(a7), one on the word at 4(a7) and one on the word at 6(a7) - which are the high and low halves of a single longword argument. So the caller passes a pair packed into one long and gets both quotients back packed the same way. Neither divide is checked for overflow.

0x1a8e0.name: add a sixteen bit script value to word 0x1a
0x1a8e0.why: assembles the value exactly as sequencerSetSlideWord does - operand low, next script byte high - and then tails into 0x1ad66, which adds it to word 0x1a rather than replacing it.

0x1a8fa.name: store the operand in the channel's level
0x1a8fa.why: 0x1a902 writes it to field 0x16, which 0x1a916 clamps to 0..0xf - four bits, and the only field this block treats that way. Skipped when byte 0x12 is 0xfe, the finishing marker.

0x1a90e.name: set bit three of the driver's change byte
0x1a90e.why: `ori.b #8,(a4)` and nothing else; a4 is the byte at 0x3e36ec the driver clears each pass and reports through. Both level handlers fall into it.

0x1a916.name: add the operand to the level and clamp it
0x1a916.why: 0x1a91e adds it to field 0x16, then 0x1a922 clears the field if the result went negative and 0x1a938 pins it at 0xf otherwise - four bits, clamped at both ends.

0x1a958.name: store the operand in field 0x19
0x1a958.why: two instructions: `move.b d4,$19(a2)` and the jump back to the sequencer. Field 0x19 is what addField5DToField19 accumulates into.

0x1a960.name: hand over to the field 0x5d adder
0x1a960.why: a single `bra.w $1ad58` - the entry inside addField5DToField19 that skips its own load of field 0x5d, so this opcode adds whatever is already in the register.

0x1a964.name: mask the operand to bits zero and three and store it in field 0x1e
0x1a964.why: `andi.b #9,d4` keeps only those two bits before `move.b d4,$1e(a2)`.

0x1a970.name: merge two operand bits into the driver's flag byte
0x1a970.why: the operand is masked to 9, the byte at 0x3e36ee is masked to 0xf6 - the complement - and the two are or'd back together, so this opcode owns exactly bits 0 and 3 of that byte.

0x1a98a.name: store the operand in field 0x20
0x1a98a.why: two instructions, like the field 0x19 opcode beside it.

0x1a9f2.name: push a loop count and the script pointer
0x1a9f2.why: refuses above five levels (0x1a9f2), then writes the operand as the count into word 0x3e and the current script pointer into long 0x3a, both indexed by depth times six, and bumps the depth at 0x25. Six bytes a level, five levels.

0x1aa28.name: count the innermost loop down or jump back to its start
0x1aa28.why: reads the top level's count at 0x3e, and if it is non-zero after decrementing restores the script pointer saved at 0x3a; when it reaches zero it drops the depth at 0x25 instead and falls through.

0x1aa5e.name: put the channel in mode two and raise the driver's mode flag
0x1aa5e.why: `0x14(a2) = 2` and `0x3e36fc = 1` - the byte setChannelSPitchNote tests to choose between its two pitch paths.

0x1aa70.name: put the channel in mode one and clear the driver's mode flag
0x1aa70.why: `0x14(a2) = 1` and 0x3e36fc cleared: the exact counterpart of the mode two opcode above it.

0x12664.name: rotate a block of entries by one, either way
0x12664.why: byte 0xf(a1) less two is the count and the sign of byte 0x10(a1) picks the direction: forwards it saves the first entry, shifts every later one down and drops the saved one at the end; backwards it does the same walking down. A colour cycle.

0x126b6.name: move each channel one step toward the target entry
0x126b6.why: masks 0x7bde7bde and 0x84218421 split an IRGB pair into the bits that may carry and the bits that may not, so all four channels can be compared and stepped in one longword. Equal channels are written straight through; the rest move by one.

0x1271e.name: blank the block once, then step only the channels that differ
0x1271e.why: the first pass through - byte 0xf(a1) still set - writes sixteen longwords of zero and clears that byte. Every pass after eors the entry with the record's target and moves only the channels the eor says are unequal.

0x12782.name: take one step off every non-zero channel of sixteen entries
0x12782.why: each of the sixteen entries has its red, green and blue fields tested and 0x400, 0x20 or 1 subtracted only where the field is not already zero, so no channel wraps. d2 stays zero if nothing moved, and the effect retires itself when it does.

0x127ca.name: take this effect off the active list and put it on the free one
0x127ca.why: the standard doubly-linked unlink through fields 0 and 4, then a push onto the list headed at 0x3e20a8. Every handler that finishes jumps here.

0x127fe.name: write one row of entries from the table and step to the next
0x127fe.why: byte 0xf(a1) entries are copied out of the table at 0x10(a1) with movep.w, then that pointer is advanced by twice the count and the countdown at 0x14(a1) is dropped.

0x12836.name: write a row, and when the countdown ends start the table again
0x12836.why: the same row write as the handler above, but it advances the table pointer by two and, when byte 0x14(a1) reaches zero, restores both the pointer and the count from the record's saved copies at 0x16 and 0x15 - so this one loops for ever where that one runs out.

0x12864.name: write one row and then unlink the effect
0x12864.why: identical row write to the two handlers above, and then a straight jump into the unlink - a one-shot.

0x12880.name: step to the next effect, or fall out when the list wraps
0x12880.why: follows field 0 to the next record and compares it against the list head; every handler in the block ends here.

0x1288a.name: restore the saved registers and return
0x1288a.why: the block's single epilogue: movem.l (a7)+ of d2-d7 and a2-a3, then rts.

0x6460.name: tell 0x2b88 about the cell, with a one
0x6460.why: pushes 1 and the routine's own word argument to 0x2b88 and goes straight to the row tail - the only case that lays no cell of its own.

0x6472.name: lay the cell, and queue a cue the first time the one below is kind 0x1a
0x6472.why: lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell on, which every case in this block does before whatever else it is for. Then it reads the cell one row down and one across - the +0x21 the board's 32-byte rows make - and if that cell's kind is 0x1a it queues a cue through the gate, but only while byte 0x14 of the record is still zero, which it then bumps by two so the cue happens once.

0x64b4.name: lay the cell and hand the argument to 0x2b74
0x64b4.why: lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell on, which every case in this block does before whatever else it is for.

0x64ce.name: ask 0x6bc0 first, then lay the cell and hand the argument to 0x2a5c
0x64ce.why: the only case that calls before it lays: 0x6bc0 gets the record and the word argument, and 0x2a5c gets the argument afterwards. lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell on, which every case in this block does before whatever else it is for.

0x64ee.name: lay the cell and hand the argument to 0x33f4
0x64ee.why: lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell on, which every case in this block does before whatever else it is for.

0x6504.name: record the coordinate on the record, lay the cell and draw its column
0x6504.why: copies the routine's two-byte word argument into field 0x3c of the record, writes the owner byte straight through with (a5)+, and then calls decompressOneColumnAdvancing with the graphic the 0/1 toggle picks out of the two-word table - the only case that draws.

0x653e.name: lay the cell and nothing else
0x653e.why: lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell on, which every case in this block does before whatever else it is for.

0x655e.name: step the walk to the next row
0x655e.why: adds 0x1000 to the screen pointer - one cell-row - flips the 0/1 toggle that chooses the graphic, and stops when the cell now under the walk equals the terminator byte.

0x657c.name: shift the last block and hand back the coordinate
0x657c.why: calls shiftEightTwoBlockS with the accumulated screen address, copies the two-byte coordinate out of the frame into the caller's record and returns it.

0x137a0.name: start the upward march over a zero background
0x137a0.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. 0x1381e clears the background, walks a bit down from 0x8000 eoring one bit at a time into each word as it goes up, then verifies on the way back down.

0x137a8.name: start the upward march over an all-ones background
0x137a8.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. 0x13822 is the same march as the one before it with the background set to 0xff instead of zero.

0x137b0.name: skip the rest when the service switch is set, otherwise march downward
0x137b0.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. It first tests bit 3 of 0x640002 and the word in d3, and jumps to the report if either says so - the only gate in the chain. Otherwise 0x13864 marches from the top of the range down, walking a bit up from 1.

0x137c6.name: march downward over an all-ones background
0x137c6.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. 0x13868 is the downward march with the background set to 0xff.

0x137ce.name: repeat the upward march over a zero background
0x137ce.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. 0x138aa is a second upward march, bit walking down from 0x8000 again, over a cleared background.

0x137d6.name: repeat the downward march over a zero background
0x137d6.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. 0x138f4 is a second downward march, bit walking up from 1, over a cleared background.

0x137de.name: fill the range with all ones
0x137de.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. It sets d0 to 0xff and re-enters the filler at 0x1380e, which writes the word up the range and mirrors each write to the test port at 0x72fffe.

0x137e8.name: repeat the upward march over an all-ones background
0x137e8.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. 0x138ae is 0x138aa with the background set to 0xff.

0x137f0.name: repeat the downward march over an all-ones background
0x137f0.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. 0x138f8 is 0x138f4 with the background set to 0xff.

0x137f8.name: invert every word, check it went to zero, then set it back
0x137f8.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. 0x13940 eors 0xffff into each word and requires the result to be zero, then ors 0xffff back in - a per-word stuck-bit check that needs no background.

0x13800.name: fill the range with zero once more
0x13800.why: the RAM test is a continuation chain: each step loads a6 with the address of the next and branches into a march, which ends `jmp (a6)`. This entry is where that chain resumes, and it is named for the march it starts rather than for its place in the queue. d0 goes back to zero and the filler runs a last time, leaving the memory clear for whatever comes after the test.

0x1380a.name: write the pattern to the test port and hand back
0x1380a.why: the chain's single exit: `move.w d0,(a3)` puts the value on the test port at 0x72fffe and `jmp (a4)` returns to whoever started the test. Every failing march jumps here too, with the eor of expected and actual in d0.

0x1a368.name: silence every channel in this group
0x1a368.why: the same sixteen-channel sweep as the handler above, matching the command's byte at 1 against byte 0x15 of each channel rather than byte 0x12 - the group field rather than the script one. silencing a channel here is always the same four writes: byte 0x5c cleared, word 0x58 set to 0x100, word 0x5a to 0xd000 and byte 0x12 to 0xfe, the finishing marker - at 0x60 bytes a channel across sixteen of them.

0x1a39a.name: stop the sample the command names
0x1a39a.why: zero-extends the command's byte at 1 and hands it to 0x1a19a, which pushes it into the ring at 0x3e3d66 and wraps the cursor - the driver's own way of queueing a stop.

0x1a3a6.name: drop the pushed argument and fall into the epilogue
0x1a3a6.why: `addq.l #4,a7` and a branch to the shared restore - the return path every handler that pushed one argument takes.

0x1a3aa.name: hand the whole command record to the routine at 0x1a3e6
0x1a3aa.why: pushes a1 itself rather than a byte out of it, which is what distinguishes this case from the ones either side.

0x1a3b0.name: ask for the sample in d2 to be started
0x1a3b0.why: zero-extends the carried sample number and calls startSampleIfPriority, which decides whether it displaces what is already playing.

0x1a3be.name: hand the command's byte to 0x1b2b2
0x1a3be.why: the same shape as the stop-sample case - byte at 1, zero-extended, one argument - but into the routine at 0x1b2b2 instead.

0x1a3ce.name: merge the command's low bits into the driver's flag byte
0x1a3ce.why: clears bits 0 and 3 of the byte at 0x3e36ee with an andi of 0xf6 and ors the command's byte at 1 back in - the same two bits the sequencer's own flag opcode owns.

0x1a3e0.name: restore the saved registers and return
0x1a3e0.why: the block's single epilogue: movem.l (a7)+ of d2-d3 and a2-a3, then rts. Every case that finds no match branches straight here.

0x27c2.name: take the graphic from the cell address lookup
0x27c2.why: calls boardCellAddressLookupWrapper with the coordinate and uses its answer as the table. every case here ends at the same tail, which reads the word at (a0) as the graphic to draw, so a case's whole job is choosing where a0 points. d3 decides between two entries of whatever table it picked.

0x27da.name: take the graphic from the table 0x3354 returns
0x27da.why: the same shape as the case above it with a different lookup. every case here ends at the same tail, which reads the word at (a0) as the graphic to draw, so a case's whole job is choosing where a0 points. d3 decides between two entries of whatever table it picked.

0x27f2.name: take the graphic from the table at 0x211d2, stepped by the cell below
0x27f2.why: d3 offsets the table by eight rather than two here, and the cell one row down - a1 plus the board's 0x20 stride - is masked to its kind and must not be 2 for the extra step. every case here ends at the same tail, which reads the word at (a0) as the graphic to draw, so a case's whole job is choosing where a0 points. d3 decides between two entries of whatever table it picked.

0x2818.name: take the graphic from the table at 0x211da
0x2818.why: the same shape as the case above with the other table. every case here ends at the same tail, which reads the word at (a0) as the graphic to draw, so a case's whole job is choosing where a0 points. d3 decides between two entries of whatever table it picked.

0x2840.name: back up over the wall run before choosing the graphic
0x2840.why: d3 takes one off the cell pointer, and if the kind there is neither 8 nor 4 it steps a whole row back - a1 less 0x20 - and raises d6. It is looking for the start of the run rather than a table.

0x285e.name: choose the graphic for a kind-eight cell from its neighbour and owner
0x285e.why: masks the cell to its kind and only proceeds when it is 8; then it reads the cell one row down and one across - the +0x21 the 32-byte rows make - takes nine off that kind and shifts the owner down six to index with.

0x28c4.name: index the table at 0x21466 by the cell's kind
0x28c4.why: masks the cell to its low six bits, takes 0x1c off, adds eight and shifts left two - four bytes an entry - into the longword table at 0x21466.

0x28e8.name: take the graphic from the pointer at 0x2133e
0x28e8.why: every case here ends at the same tail, which reads the word at (a0) as the graphic to draw, so a case's whole job is choosing where a0 points. d3 decides between two entries of whatever table it picked.

0x28fa.name: take the graphic from the pointer at 0x21342
0x28fa.why: every case here ends at the same tail, which reads the word at (a0) as the graphic to draw, so a case's whole job is choosing where a0 points. d3 decides between two entries of whatever table it picked.

0x2908.name: index by owner when there is one, otherwise build from the coordinate
0x2908.why: shifts the cell byte down six to the owner and, when that is non-zero, indexes the longword table at 0x20672 with it. When it is zero the graphic comes from the row and column instead - row less one times 0x28, column less one doubled, added to the base at 0x3e0e7a.

0x3a4a.name: draw the cell from the owner's own graphic table
0x3a4a.why: shifts the cell byte down six to the owner and does nothing when there is none; otherwise the owner times four indexes the table of tables in d3, and the word at the head of the entry it names is what gets drawn.

0x3a7e.name: draw two graphics from the pair the lookup returns
0x3a7e.why: calls 0x3cee and then boardCellAddressLookupWrapper, and draws the word at the address it answers and the word two on from it - the only case that draws twice.

0x3ac6.name: draw only when the cell's kind is the one being looked for
0x3ac6.why: reads the cell byte through a4 and compares its low six bits against the kind carried in d6; a mismatch skips the whole case.

0x3b06.name: hand the coordinate to 0x2aae
0x3b06.why: one push of the coordinate at (a2) and one call, then the shared step.

0x3b0e.name: look the record up, then pass its byte at 1 with the coordinate
0x3b0e.why: calls 0xbb38 with the coordinate, takes the byte at 1 of the record it answers, and hands that byte and the coordinate to cellNeighbourRead - the only case that passes two arguments.

0x3b2c.name: hand the coordinate to 0x2eb8
0x3b2c.why: one push and one call, then the shared step.

0x3b34.name: hand the coordinate to 0x34b2
0x3b34.why: one push and one call, then the shared step.

0x3b3c.name: advance every pointer one cell and stop at the row's end
0x3b3c.why: eight bytes on the screen pointer and d4, 0x20 on the board pointer and a4 - the board's row stride - and one on the column byte at (a2), looping back while it is under 0x2a, the board's 42 columns.

0x3b4c.name: the column counter reached 0x2a, so decide whether another row follows
0x3b4c.why: the compare that ends the row walk, falling through to the row bookkeeping when it does.

0x3b54.name: queue one of two cues when the row count reaches 0xc or 0x16
0x3b54.why: compares the row counter at -0xa(a6) against 0xc and 0x16 and queues cue 0x34 or 0x35 through the gate, then steps that counter and stops the whole walk at 0x20 rows.

0x7236.name: cue the landing, bump the player's counter and place the sprite
0x7236.why: the same landing as the case above, except that it bumps the byte at 0x17 of the player record before it asks for the graphic - the only difference between scoring and not.

0x7262.name: store the graphic the call answered and fall to the tail
0x7262.why: the join every cueing case reaches: `move.w d0,(a3)` and then the shared reset of the sprite's countdown.

0x726e.name: probe the landing square and pick the cue set from the answer
0x726e.why: only runs the probe at 0xb958 when the mode byte at 0x3e1956 is set; a zero answer or a clear mode both fall to the plain cue set, and anything else takes the scoring one.

0x72ec.name: cue, draw, then bump the player's counter by index
0x72ec.why: the counter this bumps is reached by recomputing the player record from the byte at 2 rather than from the pointer the other scoring case kept, which is the only thing that separates the two.

0x7318.name: cue, draw, and pull the sprite up and left
0x7318.why: marks the sprite dirty with bit 5 of byte 2, calls 0x404a when the code at -1(a6) is zero or 0x30, and then takes six off the sprite's y and two off its x.

0x735c.name: cue, draw and mark the sprite dirty
0x735c.why: the same as the case above without the nudge or the 0x404a call - just the ori of bit 5 into byte 2.

0x737e.name: choose the frame from a stage index, bounded at two
0x737e.why: clamps the index to 2, doubles it into the word table at 0x1f84c and asks for that graphic; a record kind of 0x25 adds ten to the answer.

0x73c0.name: leave the sprite alone
0x73c0.why: a bare branch to the tail - the case for a flier with no sprite of its own.

0x73c4.name: put five in the sprite's countdown byte
0x73c4.why: `moveq #5,d0` into byte 0xb of the sprite record, which every case falls through to.

0x10e4.name: draw the cell that belongs to a player
0x10e4.why: the owner is the cell byte shifted down six, and both it and the flag in d2 must be non-zero. The owner less one indexes the per-player table at 0x1000e, and that byte goes to cellWriteHelper with a height of eight.

0x1130.name: drop one pushed word and step on
0x1130.why: `addq.l #2,a7` and a branch to the step - the return path for the cases that pushed a single coordinate.

0x1136.name: hand the coordinate and a zero to 0x2c86
0x1136.why: two pushes and a call, then the three-word drop.

0x1142.name: hand the coordinate to 0x2e28
0x1142.why: one push and a call, then a branch past the step to the walk's other tail.

0x1150.name: strip the owner, then draw only if the kind matches the cell at a2
0x1150.why: when the flag in d2 is set it first strips the cell it is standing on down to its kind - `andi.b #$3f` through the pointer at -4(a6), which clears the owner's two bits. It then reads the byte at (a2), masks it to its low six bits and requires it to equal the owner already in d3 before it calls 0x2b88.

0x1180.name: strip the owner, then hand the coordinate on
0x1180.why: when the flag in d2 is set it first strips the cell it is standing on down to its kind - `andi.b #$3f` through the pointer at -4(a6), which clears the owner's two bits. Unlike the case above it makes the call unconditionally.

0x1196.name: strip the owner and step on
0x1196.why: when the flag in d2 is set it first strips the cell it is standing on down to its kind - `andi.b #$3f` through the pointer at -4(a6), which clears the owner's two bits. and then nothing else.

0x11a0.name: take the colour out of the owner-to-colour table and draw
0x11a0.why: the only case that reaches 0xfe02, the table that maps an owner to a colour, indexing it with the value already in d0.

0x1a992.name: push the return address and jump to a script address
0x1a992.why: refuses above five levels at 0x24(a2), then assembles a 24-bit address out of the operand and the next three script bytes and takes the script there, keeping where it came from - a call, where the loop opcode keeps a count as well.

0x1a9ea.name: set the script pointer outright
0x1a9ea.why: one instruction of work: `move.l d3,$4(a2)` puts the assembled address in the channel's script pointer with nothing saved, which is what makes it a jump rather than the call above it.

0x1aa80.name: set the key byte from the operand and post code 0xd
0x1aa80.why: byte 0x5f takes 0x10 when the operand is non-zero and 0 when it is not - a flag, not a value. d6 holds the address of the driver variable at 0x3e36da, so `movea.l d6,a0; move.l (a0),d0` reaches the record it points at; byte 6 of that record takes a small code and byte 4 the operand.

0x1aa9c.name: store the operand in field 0x18 and post code 6
0x1aa9c.why: d6 holds the address of the driver variable at 0x3e36da, so `movea.l d6,a0; move.l (a0),d0` reaches the record it points at; byte 6 of that record takes a small code and byte 4 the operand.

0x1aaba.name: post code 0xb with the operand
0x1aaba.why: d6 holds the address of the driver variable at 0x3e36da, so `movea.l d6,a0; move.l (a0),d0` reaches the record it points at; byte 6 of that record takes a small code and byte 4 the operand.

0x1aaf2.name: ask for the operand's sample to be started
0x1aaf2.why: zero-extends the operand and calls startSampleIfPriority, which decides whether it displaces what is playing.

0x1ab00.name: push the operand into the driver's stop ring
0x1ab00.why: the same one-argument shape as the start opcode above, into 0x1a19a - the ring at 0x3e3d66 whose cursor wraps at 0x3e3d61.

0x1ab10.name: silence the channel this script is running on
0x1ab10.why: the same four writes the command drain uses on a matching channel - byte 0x5c cleared, word 0x5a to 0xd000, word 0x58 to 0x100 and byte 0x12 to 0xfe - but on a2 directly rather than by index.

0x1ab2a.name: assemble the sixteen bit word at field 0x22
0x1ab2a.why: the operand is the low byte and the next script byte the high one, the same two-byte assembly the slide opcodes use, into field 0x22 instead.

0x1ab48.name: carry the operand in d3 into the routine at 0x1ac02
0x1ab48.why: two instructions and a branch; the work is all in what it hands over to.

0x1ab50.name: add the operand to field 0x18 and post code 6
0x1ab50.why: the adding counterpart of the opcode that stores into field 0x18. d6 holds the address of the driver variable at 0x3e36da, so `movea.l d6,a0; move.l (a0),d0` reaches the record it points at; byte 6 of that record takes a small code and byte 4 the operand.

0x1ab70.name: take the level from the operand's top bits and read one more byte
0x1ab70.why: shifts the operand left five and masks to 0x1f00 into word 0x58, then fetches a further script byte - so the operand carries two things at once. Skipped when byte 0x12 is 0xfe, the finishing marker.

0x1abb6.name: put the operand in word 0x1c
0x1abb6.why: moves it to d1 and tails into the sign-extending store at 0x1ace4, which writes word 0x1c.

0x1abbc.name: take the operand off word 0x1c
0x1abbc.why: moves it to d1 and tails into 0x1ad46, the subtracting counterpart of the store above.

0x1abc2.name: add the operand to field 0x5d
0x1abc2.why: one instruction before it falls into the copy of 0x5d into 0x5e that ends this whole block.

0x1398c.name: start the upward march over a zero background
0x1398c.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. 0x139fc clears the background and walks a bit down from 0x8000.

0x13994.name: start the upward march over an all-ones background
0x13994.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. 0x13a00 is the same march with the background set to 0xff.

0x1399c.name: skip the rest when the service switch is set, otherwise march downward
0x1399c.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. It tests bit 3 of 0x640002 and jumps to the report if it is set - the only gate, and unlike the first chain's it has no second condition. 0x13a44 then marches from the top down.

0x139ae.name: march downward over an all-ones background
0x139ae.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. 0x13a48 is the downward march with the background set to 0xff.

0x139b6.name: repeat the upward march over a zero background
0x139b6.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. 0x13a8a is a second upward march over a cleared background.

0x139be.name: repeat the downward march over a zero background
0x139be.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. 0x13ada is a second downward march over a cleared background.

0x139c6.name: fill the range with all ones
0x139c6.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. d0 goes to 0xff and the filler at 0x139ec runs again, mirroring each write to the test port at 0x72fffe.

0x139d0.name: repeat the upward march over an all-ones background
0x139d0.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. 0x13a8e is the ones-background twin of 0x13a8a.

0x139d8.name: repeat the downward march over an all-ones background
0x139d8.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. 0x13ade is the ones-background twin of 0x13ada.

0x139e0.name: invert every word, check it went to zero, then set it back
0x139e0.why: the second RAM test is the same continuation chain as ramTestAllPatterns and in the same order: each step loads a6 with the next and branches into a march that ends jmp (a6). This entry is named for the march it starts. 0x13b24 needs no background at all: it eors 0xffff into each word, requires zero, and ors it back.

0x139e8.name: write the pattern to the test port and hand back
0x139e8.why: the chain's single exit: the value goes to 0x72fffe and jmp (a4) returns to whoever started the test. Every failing march jumps here with the eor of expected and actual in d0.

0x92b0.name: count down, then dissolve the screen and spawn the round
0x92b0.why: the phase's own countdown is the word at -4(a6): it drops it and leaves the machine alone until it reaches zero, which is how a phase holds the screen for a while. When it does it dissolves the screen, clears the sound flag and calls entitySpawnWrapper.

0x9312.name: deal every player a starting hand and draw the prompt
0x9312.why: calls giveEachPlayerStartingHand first thing and draws a line of text with the count it answered.

0x9466.name: count down, then walk the list with the flag raised
0x9466.why: the phase's own countdown is the word at -4(a6): it drops it and leaves the machine alone until it reaches zero, which is how a phase holds the screen for a while. Then it puts the record at 0x3e1964 in place and hands it to walkWholeListFlagRaised.

0x94be.name: move to the next active player and set the phase byte to three
0x94be.why: calls advanceNextActivePlayerWrap and writes 3 to the station byte at 0x3e1958.

0x952c.name: drop eight pushed bytes and wait
0x952c.why: the return path for the case above it, which pushed two longs before its call.

0x9532.name: read the cursor unless the mode byte is six
0x9532.why: checks the byte at 0x3e0dd2 for 6 and skips the whole phase if it is; otherwise it reads the cursor coordinate and works from the record at 0x3e1cec.

0x9670.name: wait for the event at 0x11ae8
0x9670.why: waits on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero, which is this state machine's way of blocking on something the rest of the game posts.

0x96a4.name: wait for the event at 0x11b7e
0x96a4.why: waits on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero, which is this state machine's way of blocking on something the rest of the game posts. Then it drops its own countdown.

0x9722.name: walk the player array with the phase timer in hand
0x9722.why: sets d2 to 2 and d3 to 0xe, points a4 at the player array at 0x3e1968 and a3 at the phase timer byte at 0x3e1870, clearing the station byte first.

0x9860.name: walk the player array testing the status word against 0xbfff
0x9860.why: the same array walk as the phase above with d2 set to 1 and 0xbfff in d3 - the status bits less the top two - and a2 pointed at the station byte.

0x98f0.name: wait for the event at 0x11b06, then the one at 0x11b1e
0x98f0.why: waits on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero, which is this state machine's way of blocking on something the rest of the game posts.

0x999a.name: take the phase's number out of a table indexed by 0x3e0dda
0x999a.why: the byte at 0x3e0dda indexes the table at 0x117f6 and the byte it finds is what the phase runs on - the only phase whose behaviour is a table lookup rather than a fixed sequence.

0x9bd2.name: wait for the countdown, then for the event at 0x11b06
0x9bd2.why: tests the countdown at -4(a6) rather than decrementing it, and only when it has run out does it wait on the event.

0x0d0fa.name: load the level once, the first time through
0x0d0fa.why: guarded on the phase timer byte at 0x3e1870 being zero, so it runs once: start the palette sequence, set every active player up, load the level data, and then write 1 to that byte so it cannot run again.

0x0d140.name: step every shot and every unit, and wait while either is busy
0x0d140.why: adds what stepEveryShotFlightDraw and unitMovement answer and stays in the phase while the sum is non-zero; when both are idle it sets the countdown to ten.

0x0d15e.name: dissolve the screen and rebuild the playfield
0x0d15e.why: dissolves, walks the list with the flag raised, clears the palette, and blits the fixed image unless the byte at 0x3e194e says otherwise.

0x0d192.name: dissolve and hand on to phase seven with a twenty-tick wait
0x0d192.why: one dissolve, 0x14 into the countdown and 7 into the phase byte.

0x0d1a4.name: fade the palette with the level byte as its argument
0x0d1a4.why: steps the fade and passes the byte at 0x3e194e - the same byte the rebuild above tests - along with 0xffff.

0x0d1de.name: clear the framebuffer band and hand on to phase nine
0x0d1de.why: 0x168 into the countdown - a full second at sixty ticks - and 9 into the phase byte.

0x0d1ec.name: drop the pushed argument and wait
0x0d1ec.why: the return path for the phase above, which pushed one long before its call.

0x0d1f2.name: fade every bank, reset the round and deal again
0x0d1f2.why: fades all seven banks, resets the round and its queue, gives every player their own play, and sets the phase byte to 0xa.

0x0d206.name: wait on the event at 0x11b1e, then post 0x11b8a
0x0d206.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero. The phase byte at (a2) and the countdown word at (a3) are how it hands on when it does.

0x0d28c.name: scan the whole board and post the round's outcome
0x0d28c.why: counts the board's cells by type and hands the answer to endRoundPostOutcomeEvent with a one, then posts the record at 0x11b2a.

0x0d2b6.name: wait on 0x11b1e, then clear the sixteen-slot table flag
0x0d2b6.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero. The phase byte at (a2) and the countdown word at (a3) are how it hands on when it does.

0x0d2e8.name: wait on 0x11b36, then clear every player's index
0x0d2e8.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero. The phase byte at (a2) and the countdown word at (a3) are how it hands on when it does.

0x0d30c.name: wait on 0x11b8a, then post 0x11b90
0x0d30c.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero. The phase byte at (a2) and the countdown word at (a3) are how it hands on when it does.

0x0d37e.name: load the level's palettes and data, then hand on to phase sixteen
0x0d37e.why: starts the eight level palettes, clears the slot flag, loads the level data and writes 0x10 to the phase byte.

0x0d392.name: wait on 0x11b1e, then clear all eight registered handlers
0x0d392.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero. The phase byte at (a2) and the countdown word at (a3) are how it hands on when it does.

0x0d3d6.name: step every shot while waiting on 0x11b9c
0x0d3d6.why: the only phase here that does work and waits at the same time: it steps the shots each pass and keeps their count beside the event's answer.

0x0a4a0.name: drop the countdown and wait
0x0a4a0.why: the word at -4(a6) less one and straight back to the dispatcher - the shortest phase here.

0x0a4aa.name: step every shot, and the units too when the mode byte is set
0x0a4aa.why: keeps what stepEveryShotFlightDraw answers and adds unitMovement's answer to it only when the byte at 0x3e1956 is non-zero, so the phase stays put while either is busy.

0x0a548.name: post the round's outcome and set the gate word to 0x13
0x0a548.why: hands a zero to endRoundPostOutcomeEvent, writes 0x13 to the queue gate at 0x3e1948 and jumps into the main machine's own phase.

0x0a55a.name: wait on 0x11b1e, then walk the list with the flag raised
0x0a55a.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero.

0x0a586.name: wait on 0x11bc6, then post 0x11b06
0x0a586.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero.

0x0a632.name: wait on 0x11b06, then look at the phase timer
0x0a632.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero. and then tests the byte at 0x3e1870 rather than posting anything.

0x135ba.name: point the descriptor cursor back at the start of the table
0x135ba.why: two identical `lea $1325e(pc),a5` - the entry and the fall-through both reset the cursor before the walk reads its first record.

0x135c2.name: read the next descriptor and stop at the terminator
0x135c2.why: pulls a result long, a start and an end address and a flag word off the cursor, and a zero in the first stops the walk.

0x135d6.name: run the second RAM chain over this descriptor's range
0x135d6.why: sets the continuation to 0x135e0 and branches into ramTestSPassSequence.

0x135e0.name: stop on a failure, otherwise run the block test
0x135e0.why: a zero answer goes back for the next descriptor; anything else is a failure and it keeps the address before running the block test at 0x13134.

0x135f0.name: report the result according to the two switch bits
0x135f0.why: bit 0 of 0x640000 decides whether the answer reaches the test port at 0x72fffe at all, and bit 3 whether the cursor steps back a record.

0x0cc3a.name: switch on the state, keeping the low bit of the player's byte 0x19
0x0cc3a.why: the parity that gives this routine its name is `andi.w #1` on the player's byte at 0x19, kept in the frame; the five-way jump table at 0xcc0e is what runs.

0x0cc52.name: queue the cue unless bit 1 of byte 0x19 is set
0x0cc52.why: the only case that queues through passByteOnlyWhenGate, and it writes 0x46 to the marker at 0x3e1950 afterwards.

0x0cc68.name: act only when the player's byte 0x14 is two
0x0cc68.why: passes the player and the first per-player table to the gated forwarder.

0x0cc76.name: act only when the byte at the target is negative
0x0cc76.why: follows the pointer at 0x6a of the player record and tests the byte there, passing the second per-player table when it is.

0x0cc88.name: run the countdown check only on the even parity
0x0cc88.why: the word kept in the frame at the top decides it, which is what the parity was computed for.

0x0cc96.name: step to the next player and stop after three
0x0cc96.why: 0x7e on the record pointer - the player array's stride - and the count in the frame bounded at three.

0x07578.name: choose the stamp kind from the record byte
0x07578.why: 0x27 when the record's byte is 0x25 and 3 otherwise - the only thing this entry decides before the cell walk starts.

0x0759e.name: ask the cell routine about kind eight
0x0759e.why: pushes the two coordinates and an eight to the routine in a2 and keeps its answer, which is what the next entry branches on.

0x075b2.name: act when the answer was eight and the cell has an owner
0x075b2.why: requires the answer to be 8 and the cell byte's 0xc0 bits to be non-zero, so an unowned cell falls straight through.

0x0760a.name: ask the cell routine about kind 0x11
0x0760a.why: the same three-argument call as the kind-eight case with 0x11 instead, and it compares the answer against 0x11.

0x0764c.name: find the record, age its unit and answer 0x11
0x0764c.why: looks the record up by key offset, ages it a round faster, and settles the answer at 0x11.

0x07664.name: draw the entity cell one step and answer eight
0x07664.why: one call to drawEntityCellOneStep and the answer set to 8.

0x07672.name: hand the answer back
0x07672.why: zero-extends the kind into d0, restores the saved registers and returns - the single exit every case reaches.

0x00fb4.name: split the cell byte into its owner and its kind
0x00fb4.why: the 0xc0 bits into d3 and those bits shifted down six into d1 - the two halves every walk in this ROM works from, done once at the top.

0x01064.name: write kind five into the cell and push 0xb0
0x01064.why: the only case that stores a kind before it pushes; 0xb0 is what the shared tail is called with.

0x0106c.name: push 0xb0 to the shared tail
0x0106c.why: two instructions - the argument and the branch.

0x01074.name: push 0xc0 to the shared tail
0x01074.why: the same two instructions with the other value.

0x0107c.name: clear the cell byte outright, then draw
0x0107c.why: guarded on the flag in d2; it zeroes the whole byte rather than masking off the owner, which is what separates it from the case below.

0x010c8.name: strip the owner off the cell, then draw
0x010c8.why: the same guard, but an andi.b of 0x3f - the kind kept, the owner's two bits cleared.

0x1abd0.name: take the operand off field 0x5d
0x1abd0.why: the sound record's field 0x5d family: each entry applies one operation to it with the operand and then they all fall into the same copy of 0x5d into 0x5e.

0x1abd6.name: and the operand into field 0x5d
0x1abd6.why: the sound record's field 0x5d family: each entry applies one operation to it with the operand and then they all fall into the same copy of 0x5d into 0x5e.

0x1abdc.name: or the operand into field 0x5d
0x1abdc.why: the sound record's field 0x5d family: each entry applies one operation to it with the operand and then they all fall into the same copy of 0x5d into 0x5e.

0x1abe2.name: eor the operand into field 0x5d
0x1abe2.why: the sound record's field 0x5d family: each entry applies one operation to it with the operand and then they all fall into the same copy of 0x5d into 0x5e.

0x1abe8.name: fall into the copy
0x1abe8.why: a bare branch - the join the four operations share.

0x1ae44.name: work out the channel's pitch and envelope from the note
0x1ae44.why: the body of the family: it looks the note up in the table at 0x3e36de, adjusts the channel's accumulator at 0xa and 0xe, and branches on the driver's mode byte at 0x3e36fc.

0x1b048.name: the note handler's exit
0x1b048.why: an entry into the channel's note handler, which the driver reaches by tail jump; they share the same voice record in a2 and the same note and operand registers. Every path through the handler ends here.

0x1b050.name: a second exit into the same tail
0x1b050.why: an entry into the channel's note handler, which the driver reaches by tail jump; they share the same voice record in a2 and the same note and operand registers.

0x1b054.name: a third exit into the same tail
0x1b054.why: an entry into the channel's note handler, which the driver reaches by tail jump; they share the same voice record in a2 and the same note and operand registers.

0x061c2.name: take a free entry record, then lay the cell
0x061c2.why: the only case that calls takeNextFreeEntryRecord first. lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell BACK, which is the direction that separates this routine from placementCommit.

0x061e2.name: lay the cell and hand the argument to 0x33f4
0x061e2.why: lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell BACK, which is the direction that separates this routine from placementCommit.

0x061f8.name: record the coordinate on the record, then lay the cell
0x061f8.why: copies the word argument into field 0x3c of the record before laying, the same thing placementCommit's drawing case does. lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell BACK, which is the direction that separates this routine from placementCommit.

0x06232.name: lay the cell and nothing else
0x06232.why: lays the cell - the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in - and steps the walk one cell BACK, which is the direction that separates this routine from placementCommit.

0x06252.name: step the walk back one row
0x06252.why: 0x1000 off the screen pointer, one off the row byte, and the 0/1 toggle flipped - the backwards twin of placementCommit's row step.

0x0a016.name: put six in the queue gate and wait
0x0a016.why: one write of 6 to 0x3e1948, the word that decides whether queued cues are taken at all.

0x0a022.name: wait on 0x11b06, then count the board by cell type
0x0a022.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero.

0x0a0a0.name: let the countdown run out before waiting on 0x11b1e
0x0a0a0.why: tests the word at -4(a6) rather than decrementing it, and only then blocks.

0x0a2e6.name: wait on 0x11b1e, then clear all eight registered handlers
0x0a2e6.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero.

0x0a392.name: walk the player array posting 0x11b06
0x0a392.why: d2 set to 3, the array at 0x3e1968 in a4, the station byte cleared, and the record to post kept in d3.

0x0a752.name: step to the next player's row of the operator menu
0x0a752.why: 0x7e on the record pointer - the player array's stride - and one on the station byte at 0x3e1958.

0x0a75e.name: run the operator menu for the row the station byte names
0x0a75e.why: the byte at 0x3e1954 less one and the current record are what it hands to operatorMenu.

0x0a794.name: wait on the event at 0x11ba2
0x0a794.why: blocks on an event: it asks eventTest for a record and does nothing until the answer is zero.

0x0a7d6.name: drop twelve pushed bytes and return
0x0a7d6.why: the exit for the paths that pushed three arguments; it falls into the shared restore.

0x0a7da.name: restore the saved registers and return
0x0a7da.why: the single epilogue this whole block shares: movem.l of d2-d6 and a2-a4, unlk, rts.

0x0666c.name: load the walk's constants and start the first row
0x0666c.why: 0xb0 and 0xc0 into d2 and d3 - the two cell values this lays - seven into the nibble counter and the row byte cleared.

0x06680.name: decide whether this cell is on the board's edge
0x06680.why: row and column both non-zero and the column not 0x29 - the board's 42 columns less one - which is what keeps the border out of the fill.

0x0669c.name: take the next nibble out of the stream
0x0669c.why: masks the source byte to 0xf and uses it as the cell's value, which is what makes this a nibble stream rather than a byte one.

0x195d4.name: write the digits backwards from the end of the buffer
0x195d4.why: puts the terminator at the far end and then walks back, shifting the value down four bits a digit and adding 0x30 - ASCII zero - to each nibble.

0x19604.name: restore the saved registers and return
0x19604.why: the converter's exit; the pad loop below it falls in here too.

0x00e82.name: turn the row and column into a cell address and a screen address
0x00e82.why: the head of each row: the packed coordinate goes to cellAddress for the board pointer and to screenAddress for where it draws.

0x00efc.name: skip the cells on the board's border
0x00efc.why: row and column both non-zero, the row not 0x1d and the column not its own limit - the four tests that keep the edge out of the run.

0x011ea.name: step every pointer to the next row
0x011ea.why: 0x20 on the board pointer and the three cell pointers - the board's 32-byte row stride - and two on the screen offset.

0x01204.name: the column reached its limit, so start the next row
0x01204.why: compares the column byte against lastColumn and goes back for another cell while it is under it.

0x01214.name: the row reached its limit, so the walk is over
0x01214.why: compares the row byte against the last row in the frame and falls into the epilogue when it is past.

0x01222.name: restore the saved registers and return

0x09db2.name: drop twenty pushed bytes and carry on
0x09db2.why: the return path for the case above it, which pushed five arguments.

0x09dba.name: award unless the round byte is already three
0x09dba.why: the byte at 0x3e1ae2 is the round, and a three skips the whole award.

0x09e48.name: set the phase timer to fifteen and draw the award line
0x09e48.why: phaseTimerSet with 0xf and then textLineDraw - the pair that puts an award on screen for a fixed time.

0x09e74.name: give every player their own play and clear the posting routines
0x09e74.why: sets the queue gate at 0x3e1948 to eight, and when d5 says so removes every routine posting the record at 0x11b3c.

0x0bbd2.name: walk the ring the current record's field 0x2c names
0x0bbd2.why: the current record is the pointer at 0x3e1c84, which every entry here starts from. This one follows the pointer at 0x2c and starts two bytes in.

0x0bd84.name: walk from the current record's field 0x34 over fourteen entries
0x0bd84.why: the current record is the pointer at 0x3e1c84, which every entry here starts from. It takes the long at 0x34 and works against the table at 0x3e1bc6 with a count of fourteen.

0x0bf00.name: post 0x11b6c unless the counter at 0x3e1cac is positive
0x0bf00.why: the only entry here that starts with a test of that byte rather than with the current record.

0x0bfea.name: walk the ring against the table at 0xfcca
0x0bfea.why: the current record is the pointer at 0x3e1c84, which every entry here starts from. It keeps that table in a3 and the current-record pointer itself in a4, following 0x2c as the first entry does.

0x18806.name: step one slot's counters when its active byte is set
0x18806.why: byte 0x18 indexed by the slot number gates it; the slot's own words at 0x1c and 0x24 are then read and advanced, two bytes a slot.

0x18b3e.name: draw what the buffer already holds
0x18b3e.why: pushes the same -0x10(a6) buffer with a coordinate pair taken from bytes of its own arguments; the formatting has already happened.

0x18e02.name: find a free slot among four and fill it
0x18e02.why: walks down from 0x19(a2)+3 in the state block at 0x3e3400 looking for a clear byte, and the kind the caller chose is what goes in.

0x061a8.name: lay the cell and step back
0x061a8.why: the value masked to its low six bits with the owner's 0xc0 or'd in, then one cell back - the same lay every walk of this shape does, with nothing else.

0x066e0.name: wrap to the next column when the row reaches thirty
0x066e0.why: 0x1e is the board's 30 rows; when the row byte hits it the screen pointer is wound back 0x1e000 and eight forward, which is one column across.

0x0d440.name: drop the countdown, and step shots and units in phase four
0x0d440.why: the countdown at (a3) always drops; the two calls happen only when the phase byte at (a2) is 4.

0x130d2.name: run the second RAM chain and judge its answer
0x130d2.why: sets the continuation and branches into ramTestSPassSequence, then tests what comes back.

0x18902.name: finish the slot loop and return
0x18902.why: the dbra that closes the four-slot walk, then the restore and rts.

0x1ac3c.name: advance the script pointer by field 0x5d times four less one
0x1ac3c.why: shifts the byte at 0x5d left two and takes one off before adding it to the pointer at 4(a2) - a relative jump whose distance is a field.

0x011de.name: strip the owner off the cell, then step
0x011de.why: guarded on the flag in d2; an andi.b of 0x3f through the pointer at -4(a6) keeps the kind and clears the owner's two bits.

0x01aea.name: post one event for every player whose status word says it is live
0x01aea.why: walks the array at 0x3e1968 with the record at 0x11aee, the 0x30c stride between the two pointers it writes into fields 0x6e and 0x72, and counts what it posted.

0x022ba.name: spawn an entity for each of the three players
0x022ba.why: the array at 0x3e1968 in a3 with a count of three, a kind of one, and the table at 0x3e02d8 in a2; the answer is how many it spawned.

0x025c2.name: work out the wall's neighbours and draw its column
0x025c2.why: reads its three arguments off the stack, hands the cell address to wallCellSet, and passes what comes back to decompressOneColumnAdvancing as the graphic.

0x037e8.name: run the cell walk over the whole board
0x037e8.why: pushes the board's own limits - 0x1d rows and 0x29 columns, both the last index rather than the count - with zeros for the rest, so this is the walk applied to everything.

0x039c2.name: take the unit's colour from the owner-to-colour table
0x039c2.why: splits the cell byte into its kind and its owner and uses the owner to index 0xfe02, the same table drawPanelPlayerNothingNegative reads.

0x04c80.name: schedule the palette effect with three, three and one
0x04c80.why: keeps schedulePaletteEffectOne's address in a2 and pushes a fixed argument set - 3, 3, 1 - so what it is is entirely in those constants.
